NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe.

Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.

"The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance."
The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond.

On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn.

"Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries.

"And then, as Voyager 1 continued out to the Saturn system, it actually discovered that Saturn's large moon Titan has a very thick atmosphere surrounding it," she added. "So it's one of the only moons that has a thick atmosphere."

Decades later, Voyager 1's data is still incredibly important for scientists studying the planets and moons of our cosmic neighborhood. Phillips works on Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's ocean moon Europa. And the basis of that work stems from early observations by Voyager.

"Every time I get to use data from Voyager, I have to kind of think back to where that data came from," Phillips said. "I think about kind of the legacy, the missions that really set the precedent for a mission like Europa Clipper. Voyager is right there at the top of the list. And some of those images that we took with the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft of Europa — they're actually still, for some portions of Europa, they're the best pictures that we have. So, we're still using that data today, almost 50 years later."

Today, Voyager 1 and 2 are both exploring interstellar space. On Aug. 25, 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to leave the heliosphere, or the protective bubble of solar particles that surrounds the planets and other objects in our solar system. After crossing that boundary, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space and has been exploring the interstellar medium ever since. Voyager 2 followed suit in November 2018.

While the Voyager spacecraft have left the heliosphere, they have technically not left the solar system, as they are still within the gravitational influence of the sun. Today, Voyager 1 is traveling 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) through interstellar space, exploring farther than any human-made object in history.

The Voyager mission team communicates with Voyager in radio waves via the Deep Space Network, a collective of giant radio antennas that NASA uses to "talk" to a wide range of far-off spacecraft. And since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours for communications to reach Voyager 1, and then another 24 hours for any response to return.

"You need to have patience because now, if you send a command to Voyager, Voyager receives that command 24 hours later," Spilker said. "So two days later, you receive confirmation that yes, Voyager one received your command and is sending back the information that you'd like it to send back."

That patience is important, as the nearly-50-year-old Voyager mission is still actively making science observations and collecting new data. While some of the probes' science instruments have had to be shut off over the years to save battery life, both probes are still going strong.

"It is always difficult when an instrument has to get turned off, knowing that it has returned good science data for so many years," Spilker said. "But a plan was laid down to make sure we had at least one instrument operating on each spacecraft, one type of instrument, for as long as we could."

As long as the mission is active, the team will continue to investigate the unknown with Voyager. After all, ever since the probes entered interstellar space, they have been exploring areas of space that we've only ever studied remotely or in theory.

"Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, and what we knew about interstellar space at that point really came just from remote observations and theories. And so, right away, Voyager started to find that what we expected was not exactly right," Spilker said.

So far, the team has found that the sun's influence extends much farther from the heliopause than they expected. The Voyagers have observed and measured "ripples coming from the sun," as Spilker described them, deep in interstellar space.

"Voyager is going to continue to measure the cosmic rays and particles, and also the radio waves coming from interstellar space and coming from the sun," Spilker said, adding that the team is always eagerly "waiting to see if there might be more surprises out there."
How has this mission from the 1970s continued to not just survive but actively push forward through all of that time, overcoming countless hurdles and unexpected challenges?

"Voyager's longevity is really a tribute to all of the people who worked on Voyager, from those who designed the spacecraft, built it, programmed its computers, launched it, and then the teams of individuals that have flown it over that 50 years," Spilker said.

Spilker is a longtimeVoyager veteran. Fresh out of school, she started her NASA career with Voyager, working on the mission for about a decade before moving on to NASA's Cassini Saturn mission. After Cassini concluded with a dramatic death dive into Saturn in 2017, Spilker returned to Voyager, where she serves as a project scientist today.
"I'm very proud and happy to work on Voyager," she said.

The Voyager team is small, with just eight to 10 people on the flight team, according to Spilker. But they often bring in retired scientists and Voyager team members from decades past who are eager to share their knowledge and connect with the new generation of mission scientists and engineers.

"Voyager is multi-generational," Spilker shared. "We have someone whose parents weren't born when Voyager was launched, and then we just celebrated the 90th birthday of one of the members who retired and came back. He actually helped to build and program the computers on Voyager."

Looking to the future, the team is pressing on full speed ahead to continue science with Voyager. Another big milestone is just ahead, when the mission turns 50 this upcoming year. And Spilker is optimistic that this will not be the end.
"I see the 50th anniversary as just a milestone," Spilker said. "The next milestone, and then we'll just keep on going."

As Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, you might wonder whenVoyager 2 will hit the same milestone. Since Voyager 2 is on a slower trajectory,it won't reach one light-day from Earth until 2035, nearly a decade into the future. The Voyagers are both hardy and tough, so it's not crazy to think the probe may still be alive when it crosses that threshold.

coreStoryFacts.text: NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today.
It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.
These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming.
So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds.
For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth.
Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet.
Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds.
There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat.
Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store.
On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over.
NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor.
We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.
Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record .
Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message.

Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.

facts.text: NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today.
It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.
These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming.
So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds.
For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth.
Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet.
Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds.
There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat.
Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store.
On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over.
NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor.
We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.
Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record .
Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message.

Here’s how it works . NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance. There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers). These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away. On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though. Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record . Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet. If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received. NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.

There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).

These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.

On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.

Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record . Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.
If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.

Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

passages: After traveling for 49 years, two months and 11 days, it's now believed to be about 16 billion miles from our planet—and it's not done yet.
Voyager 1 is headed toward a star called Gliese 445, about 17 light-years from Earth in the Ursa Minor constellation.
In terms of space distances, that's not so far away.
NASA expects it to have reached that milestone at 5:16:07 AM Eastern time today, November 18.
One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in a day.
Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours to send a command to the probe and 24 hours to get a message back.
Voyager 1 headed to space in 1977 as part of NASA's program to study not just our Solar System, but also interstellar space.
It was launched 16 days after Voyager 2, but it has since traveled farther than its twin and any other probe we've sent out.
It suffered technical glitches , and NASA had to shut down some of its features to keep it going despite the diminishing plutonium in its generator.
But it's still around and hasn't stopped its journey.

sources.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
passages: After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours.
It’s the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet.

NASA has done well to keep it functioning, and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft.

It’s been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of 1 light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

passages: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe.

The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov.
EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.
The Voyagers are both hardy and tough, so it's not crazy to think the probe may still be alive when it crosses that threshold.
"The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com.
"Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active.
The Voyager mission team communicates with Voyager in radio waves via the Deep Space Network, a collective of giant radio antennas that NASA uses to "talk" to a wide range of far-off spacecraft.
"Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, and what we knew about interstellar space at that point really came just from remote observations and theories.
And so, right away, Voyager started to find that what we expected was not exactly right," Spilker said.
25, 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to leave the heliosphere, or the protective bubble of solar particles that surrounds the planets and other objects in our solar system.
"Every time I get to use data from Voyager, I have to kind of think back to where that data came from," Phillips said.
"I think about kind of the legacy, the missions that really set the precedent for a mission like Europa Clipper.
Voyager is right there at the top of the list.
And some of those images that we took with the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft of Europa — they're actually still, for some portions of Europa, they're the best pictures that we have.
So, we're still using that data today, almost 50 years later."
Fresh out of school, she started her NASA career with Voyager, working on the mission for about a decade before moving on to NASA's Cassini Saturn mission.
After Cassini concluded with a dramatic death dive into Saturn in 2017, Spilker returned to Voyager, where she serves as a project scientist today.
The Voyagers have observed and measured "ripples coming from the sun," as Spilker described them, deep in interstellar space.
Phillips works on Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's ocean moon Europa.
And the basis of that work stems from early observations by Voyager.
The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis.
It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn.
After all, ever since the probes entered interstellar space, they have been exploring areas of space that we've only ever studied remotely or in theory.
The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977.
"You need to have patience because now, if you send a command to Voyager, Voyager receives that command 24 hours later," Spilker said.
"So two days later, you receive confirmation that yes, Voyager one received your command and is sending back the information that you'd like it to send back."
That patience is important, as the nearly-50-year-old Voyager mission is still actively making science observations and collecting new data.
While some of the probes' science instruments have had to be shut off over the years to save battery life, both probes are still going strong.

"Voyager's longevity is really a tribute to all of the people who worked on Voyager, from those who designed the spacecraft, built it, programmed its computers, launched it, and then the teams of individuals that have flown it over that 50 years," Spilker said.
"I'm very proud and happy to work on Voyager," she said.
The Voyager team is small, with just eight to 10 people on the flight team, according to Spilker.
But they often bring in retired scientists and Voyager team members from decades past who are eager to share their knowledge and connect with the new generation of mission scientists and engineers.
"Voyager is multi-generational," Spilker shared.
He actually helped to build and program the computers on Voyager."
Looking to the future, the team is pressing on full speed ahead to continue science with Voyager.

So, we're still using that data today, almost 50 years later." Today, Voyager 1 and 2 are both exploring interstellar space. Today, Voyager 1 is traveling 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) through interstellar space, exploring farther than any human-made object in history. And since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours for communications to reach Voyager 1, and then another 24 hours for any response to return. "You need to have patience because now, if you send a command to Voyager, Voyager receives that command 24 hours later," Spilker said. "So two days later, you receive confirmation that yes, Voyager one received your command and is sending back the information that you'd like it to send back." That patience is important, as the nearly-50-year-old Voyager mission is still actively making science observations and collecting new data. While some of the probes' science instruments have had to be shut off over the years to save battery life, both probes are still going strong. "It is always difficult when an instrument has to get turned off, knowing that it has returned good science data for so many years," Spilker said. "But a plan was laid down to make sure we had at least one instrument operating on each spacecraft, one type of instrument, for as long as we could." As long as the mission is active, the team will continue to investigate the unknown with Voyager. After all, ever since the probes entered interstellar space, they have been exploring areas of space that we've only ever studied remotely or in theory. "Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, and what we knew about interstellar space at that point really came just from remote observations and theories. And so, right away, Voyager started to find that what we expected was not exactly right," Spilker said. So far, the team has found that the sun's influence extends much farther from the heliopause than they expected. The Voyagers have observed and measured "ripples coming from the sun," as Spilker described them, deep in interstellar space. "Voyager is going to continue to measure the cosmic rays and particles, and also the radio waves coming from interstellar space and coming from the sun," Spilker said, adding that the team is always eagerly "waiting to see if there might be more surprises out there." How has this mission from the 1970s continued to not just survive but actively push forward through all of that time, overcoming countless hurdles and unexpected challenges? "Voyager's longevity is really a tribute to all of the people who worked on Voyager, from those who designed the spacecraft, built it, programmed its computers, launched it, and then the teams of individuals that have flown it over that 50 years," Spilker said. Spilker is a longtimeVoyager veteran. Fresh out of school, she started her NASA career with Voyager, working on the mission for about a decade before moving on to NASA's Cassini Saturn mission. After Cassini concluded with a dramatic death dive into Saturn in 2017, Spilker returned to Voyager, where she serves as a project scientist today. "I'm very proud and happy to work on Voyager," she said. The Voyager team is small, with just eight to 10 people on the flight team, according to Spilker. But they often bring in retired scientists and Voyager team members from decades past who are eager to share their knowledge and connect with the new generation of mission scientists and engineers. "Voyager is multi-generational," Spilker shared. "We have someone whose parents weren't born when Voyager was launched, and then we just celebrated the 90th birthday of one of the members who retired and came back. He actually helped to build and program the computers on Voyager." Looking to the future, the team is pressing on full speed ahead to continue science with Voyager. Another big milestone is just ahead, when the mission turns 50 this upcoming year. And Spilker is optimistic that this will not be the end. "I see the 50th anniversary as just a milestone," Spilker said. "The next milestone, and then we'll just keep on going." As Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, you might wonder whenVoyager 2 will hit the same milestone. Since Voyager 2 is on a slower trajectory,it won't reach one light-day from Earth until 2035, nearly a decade into the future. The Voyagers are both hardy and tough, so it's not crazy to think the probe may still be alive when it crosses that threshold. sources.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
passages: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI.
The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot.
The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now.
Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user).
Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months.

The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.

The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data.
Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history.
That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history.
Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation.
You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training.
You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini.
That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps.
Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models.
The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles.
However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted.

sources.title: Your Google Gemini Data Is Being Used For A Lot More Than Just Sending You Ads - BGR
passages: You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account.
Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.
It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example.

When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly.
But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady.

This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ).

Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information.

extraction.body: In the ever-continuing saga of consumer data being harvested and put to use in ways people might not have intended, AI technologies present a unique source of that information. Chats and conversations you have with them, questions you ask, information you share, it's all being ingested. Google, for example, is using your regular search data to train AI . Platforms like ChatGPT regularly scoop up user data, as well. Moreover, a Stanford study found six U.S. companies with AI services that not only train systems with collected data, but also retain the information indefinitely. The study suggests that when you use something like Google Gemini, all the information it's learning and storing is feeding into something more, likely well beyond personalized ads. In Google's words, it uses the data to provide and maintain services, develop new ones, personalize them, communicate with customers, measure performance, and protect Google, users, and the public. If the targeted advertising seems the most alarming, that's because it certainly feels like your phone, or someone on the other side, is listening. However, they're so accurate because of the troves of private information companies have collected about you. The data comes from a combination of companies and data brokers, companies that profit from the aggregation, disclosure, and sale of personal information. It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example. And as Google explains, all of it is being used for much more than targeted ads. Google says your Gemini app chats "are not being used to show you ads," and maintains that it doesn't train AI with your data. It's always healthy to approach these claims with a degree of skepticism. Not because the companies involved may be outright lying to you, though they certainly do at times, but because the reality is not black and white. Google's claims specifically are only half true. This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ). Looking at the facts, Google's AI models can be trained on Gemini inputs and outputs, which might include email snippets or context, Google Workspace files, and other Google products data. Gemini app chats might not be used in this way, but other data is, including emails you feed through the service. When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly. But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady. The sheer amount of data collected from Gemini alone is concerning, especially with it now taking over Android phones and mobile devices by default. Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information. There's also the information "you provide" to Gemini, like what you say to it, what you share, transcripts and recordings of interactions, including video, audio, screens you share, and much, much more. It's an uncomfortable truth about using Google Gemini , but there are some huge privacy trade-offs. Google also says in the section about how it uses all that data that human reviewers may preview some of that information. It even advises against entering confidential information or anything sensitive that "you wouldn't want a reviewer to see" or anything you wouldn't want "Google to use to improve [its] services, including machine-learning technologies." It's also unclear how long some of the data it collects is retained. Google does share timelines, but it varies depending on what the data is and how it's used. Chats are stored for up to 72 hours, while app data can be stored for up to 18 months. You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account. Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.

extraction.body: A few weeks ago, Google DeepMind released Gemini 2.0 for everyone , including Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite, and Gemini 2.0 Pro (Experimental). All models support up to at least 1 million input tokens, which makes it easier to do a lot of things – from image generation to creative writing. It’s also changed how we convert documents into structured data. Manual document processing is a slow and expensive problem, but Gemini 2.0 changed everything when it comes to chunking pdfs for RAG systems, and can even transform pdfs into insights . Today, we'll take a deep dive into a multi-step approach using generative AI where you can use Gemini 2.0 to improve your document extraction by combining language models (LLMs) with structured, externalized rules. A multi-step architecture, as opposed to relying on a single, monolithic prompt, offers significant advantages for robust extraction. This approach begins with modular extraction, where initial tasks are broken down into smaller, more focused prompts targeting specific content locations within a document. This modularity not only enhances accuracy but also reduces the cognitive load on the LLM. Another benefit of a multi-step approach is externalized rule management. By managing post-processing rules externally, for instance, using Google Sheets or a BigQuery table, we gain the benefits of easy CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations, improving both maintainability and version control of the rules. This decoupling also separates the logic of extraction from the logic of processing, allowing for independent modification and optimization of each. Ultimately, this hybrid approach combines the strengths of LLM-powered extraction with a structured rules engine. LLMs handle the complexities of understanding and extracting information from unstructured data, while the rules engine provides a transparent and manageable system for enforcing business logic and decision-making. The following steps outline a practical implementation. Build and test your proof of concept with $300 in free credit for new customers. Plus, all customers get free monthly usage of 20+ products, including AI APIs. Let's test a sample prompt with a configurable set of rules. This hands-on example will demonstrate how easily you can define and apply business logic to extracted data, all powered by the Gemini and Vertex AI . First, we extract data from a document. Let’s use Google’s 2023 Environment Report as the source document. We use Gemini with the initial prompt to extract data. This is not a known schema, but a prompt we’ve created for the purposes of this story. To create specific response schemas, use controlled generation with Gemini . The JSON output below, which we'll assign to the variable ` extracted_data `, represents the results of the initial data extraction by Gemini. This structured data is now ready for the next critical phase: applying our predefined business rules. Next, we'll feed this ` extracted_data ` into a rules engine, which, in our implementation, is another call to Gemini, acting as a powerful and flexible rules processor. Along with the extracted data, we'll provide a set of validation rules defined in the ` analysis_rules ` variable. This engine, powered by Gemini, will systematically check the extracted data for accuracy, consistency, and adherence to our predefined criteria. Below is the prompt we provide to Gemini to accomplish this, along with the rules themselves. ` analysis_rules ` is a JSON object that contains the business rules we want to apply to the extracted receipt data. Each rule defines a specific condition to check, an action to take if the condition is met, and an optional alert message if a violation occurs. The power of this approach lies in the flexibility of these rules; you can easily add, modify, or remove them without altering the core extraction process. The beauty of using Gemini is that the rules can be written in human-readable language and can be maintained by non-coders. Finally – and crucially – integrate the alerts and insights generated by the rules engine into existing data pipelines and workflows. This is where the real value of this multi-step process is unlocked. For our example, we can build robust APIs and systems using Google Cloud tools to automate downstream actions triggered by the rule-based analysis. Some examples of downstream tasks are: Automated task creation: Trigger Cloud Functions to create tasks in project management systems, assigning data verification to the appropriate teams. Data quality pipelines: Integrate with Dataflow to flag potential data inconsistencies in BigQuery tables, triggering validation workflows. Vertex AI integration: Leverage Vertex AI Model Registry for tracking data lineage and model performance related to extracted metrics and corrections made. Dashboard integration Use Looker, Google Sheets, or Data Studio to display alerts Human in the loop trigger: Build a trigger system for the Human in the loop, using Cloud Tasks, to show which extractions to focus on and double check. This hands-on approach provides a solid foundation for building robust, rule-driven document extraction pipelines. To get started, explore these resources: Gemini for document understanding: For a comprehensive, one-stop solution to your document processing needs, check out Gemini for document understanding . It simplifies many common extraction challenges. Few-shot prompting: Begin your Gemini journey with few-shot prompting . This powerful technique can significantly improve the quality of your extractions with minimal effort, providing examples within the prompt itself. Fine-tuning Gemini models: When you need highly specialized, domain-specific extraction results, consider fine-tuning Gemini models . This allows you to tailor the model's performance to your exact requirements.

coreStoryFacts.text: “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email.
Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI.
But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history.
Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback.
In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history.
Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly.
I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction.
To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings.
(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
© 2026 ZDNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.
Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI.
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI.
The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot.
The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now.
Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user).
Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months.

The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.

The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data.
Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history.
That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history.
Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation.
You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training.

extraction.body: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. sources.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
passages: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI.
The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot.
The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now.
Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user).
Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months.

The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.

The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data.
Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history.
That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history.
Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation.
You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training.
You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini.
That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps.
Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models.
The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles.
However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted.
Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement.

passages: You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account.
Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.
It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example.

When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly.
But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady.

This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ).

Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information.

extraction.body: In the ever-continuing saga of consumer data being harvested and put to use in ways people might not have intended, AI technologies present a unique source of that information. Chats and conversations you have with them, questions you ask, information you share, it's all being ingested. Google, for example, is using your regular search data to train AI . Platforms like ChatGPT regularly scoop up user data, as well. Moreover, a Stanford study found six U.S. companies with AI services that not only train systems with collected data, but also retain the information indefinitely. The study suggests that when you use something like Google Gemini, all the information it's learning and storing is feeding into something more, likely well beyond personalized ads. In Google's words, it uses the data to provide and maintain services, develop new ones, personalize them, communicate with customers, measure performance, and protect Google, users, and the public. If the targeted advertising seems the most alarming, that's because it certainly feels like your phone, or someone on the other side, is listening. However, they're so accurate because of the troves of private information companies have collected about you. The data comes from a combination of companies and data brokers, companies that profit from the aggregation, disclosure, and sale of personal information. It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example. And as Google explains, all of it is being used for much more than targeted ads. Google says your Gemini app chats "are not being used to show you ads," and maintains that it doesn't train AI with your data. It's always healthy to approach these claims with a degree of skepticism. Not because the companies involved may be outright lying to you, though they certainly do at times, but because the reality is not black and white. Google's claims specifically are only half true. This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ). Looking at the facts, Google's AI models can be trained on Gemini inputs and outputs, which might include email snippets or context, Google Workspace files, and other Google products data. Gemini app chats might not be used in this way, but other data is, including emails you feed through the service. When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly. But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady. The sheer amount of data collected from Gemini alone is concerning, especially with it now taking over Android phones and mobile devices by default. Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information. There's also the information "you provide" to Gemini, like what you say to it, what you share, transcripts and recordings of interactions, including video, audio, screens you share, and much, much more. It's an uncomfortable truth about using Google Gemini , but there are some huge privacy trade-offs. Google also says in the section about how it uses all that data that human reviewers may preview some of that information. It even advises against entering confidential information or anything sensitive that "you wouldn't want a reviewer to see" or anything you wouldn't want "Google to use to improve [its] services, including machine-learning technologies." It's also unclear how long some of the data it collects is retained. Google does share timelines, but it varies depending on what the data is and how it's used. Chats are stored for up to 72 hours, while app data can be stored for up to 18 months. You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account. Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.

extraction.body: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre I n GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. For a long time you really are two-bit criminals on the run, getting in with every dirtbag petty thief and drug-runner you come across in order to scrape some cash together and stay under the radar. You meet hillbilly pill-heads and biker gangs, friendly conspiracy theorists, a shady doctor, Lucia’s former prison friends and their lowlife boyfriends. By the time I actually got to Vice City – a glitzy den of sin, the centre of all Leonida’s pleasures and all its most extravagant criminality, where the gangbangers hustle on social media and even the narcos are obsessed with their Instagram clout – I had been playing for 30 hours. It took me 70 hours to finish the game and I could have taken longer. Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please. There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself. I often felt that the only thing messing up Rockstar’s perfect simulation was me. All this detail and realism comes with some disadvantages, namely complex controls and a tendency for the game’s systems to collide with my intentions in unexpected and sometimes annoying ways. Here I am, driving at high speed through the city before clipping the kerb and flipping my car, causing a massive pile-up. Here I am pressing the wrong button and accidentally punching a random passerby rather than greeting them as intended, kicking off a ridiculous skirmish in which I have to knock out half the customers at a restaurant before running from the cops. Here I am again pressing the wrong button at a bike rack and ending up pinned beneath a tumbling row of bicycles. Missions can go south very quickly and for reasons that aren’t always obvious. In every street race I wiped out spectacularly by crashing into something I couldn’t properly see, while my opponents magically recovered from every collision and sped ahead. This can be a frustrating game at times: unpredictable, laborious, unwieldy and, occasionally, unfair. That is because you are not the master of the game world. You simply exist within it. Like most compelling crime fiction, Jason and Lucia’s story involves an escalating series of messy events that pull them further and further from where they started, and have you constantly wondering how on earth they’re going to get out of the newest trouble they’re in. To avoid spoilers, substantive discussion of this story can only happen in the coming weeks. But I will say that I was rooting so hard for Jason and Lucia by the end that I felt quite sick with worry about what was going to happen to them, pacing back and forth in front of my TV throughout the final missions. Among all the expectations I had for GTA VI, I did not expect it to make me so emotional. The key to this is the bond you form with Jason and Lucia. After tens of hours in their company, watching them together – how she smiles fondly at him when they dance together, their playful banter, the stick-ups they pull off as a duo, their resilience and faith in themselves and each other in the face of escalating disaster – I found it impossible not to care for them. They are our avatars in GTA VI’s world but they are not blank stand-ins for the player: you decide their actions but not their personalities. They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim. It made me care about them much more. When the story gave me opportunities to decide what would happen next, what came to mind for me was what they would do, not what I would do. This is indicative of a tonal shift for Grand Theft Auto that became more obvious the more I played. This series is famous for its violence, misanthropy and pitch-black humour. I have been invested in its characters before, have even rooted for some of them, but I have rarely liked them or related to them. This is the first GTA that wants to encourage some measure of empathy alongside its trademark violent chaos. I was astonished to discover that the game offers you small incentives for acts of kindness, such as texting your partner a selfie, doing your neighbour a favour or throwing your rubbish in the bin rather than dropping it on the ground. Jason and Lucia are not extravagant caricatures, but two people trying to make it in a world totally stacked against them. Pretty much everyone in this Floridian fever-dream is a total crook, on the take or mixed up in some bullshit scheme. It’s so easy to get away with crime in this city, and so difficult to do things the right way. The events of this game might be totally outlandish but these characters and their motivations keep things at least somewhat grounded. If you thought this newfound heart might tone down GTA’s 18-rated provocativeness, however, you would be very wrong. The protagonists may be surprisingly relatable but they exist in a world that is absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive in every imaginable way. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Barely a half-hour ever goes by without someone snorting coke off a knife blade, or some full-frontal nudity. There are missions set inside a pornographer’s mansion and a small-town strip club; you can visit those clubs and get a private dance (as either Jason or Lucia, for what it’s worth, or together). At one point Lucia opens the wrong hotel room door to see a woman in a corset wielding a golf club, thwacking balls at a guy’s testicles. On the in-game TV there is a reality show about horny geriatrics. It does not so much push the boundaries of taste as ignore the existence of taste. It contains every perverted scenario you could imagine and several more that would never occur to you. Sometimes it is a little jarring to emerge from a really pivotal and moving scene between Jason and Lucia into a virtual city where the billboards read things like “WANTED for shitting everywhere: THE SHIT BEAST.” But I found these two sides of GTA’s personality surprisingly easy to accommodate. It’s not as though the story is without its many moments of absurd levity and humour, too: at one point I was taking a bunch of terrifying gang leaders with face tattoos on a real-estate tour, where they sincerely admired the outdoor space with brick pizza oven, and another time I was chasing a man wearing nothing but an alligator thong through a well-to-do suburban neighbourhood. A game this huge can accommodate both pathos and lewdness, and much more. I did find, however, that Lucia – Grand Theft Auto’s first female protagonist – changed how a lot of this landed for me. GTA has never been particularly kind to women (or men, for that fact, but in past games it has exclusively been the women who were sexualised). There is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI’s world, but now we have Lucia to react to it. This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story, from up-and-coming rappers to Lucia’s mother, from a jaded strip-club worker to a badass middle-aged drug-runner whose custom purple carbine rifle is her prized possession. This is a game in which women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men. And without wanting to give too much away: there are male strippers in Leonida, too. I am not about to make a case for GTA VI as a feminist game – there is much to be offended by here, if you are so inclined – but I will say that as a woman who has played and enjoyed every GTA game while also often rolling my eyes at their casual sniggering misogyny, GTA VI hits different for me. I liked it more because the women aren’t always the butt of a joke. Also for the first time, I did not find the violence gratuitous or overblown, despite the fact that this is a story about crime and criminals. There is nothing here like GTA V’s infamous torture mission , which made me feel sick. It says a lot that of all the immoral opportunities afforded to me in Vice City, the only thing I straight-up said “no” to was getting involved in a metaverse scam. THAT would be going too far. I keep reaching for something that sums up GTA VI, as much as it’s possible to sum up a game as vast as this, and the closest I come is the nightclubs. These show GTA VI at its most extravagant: hundreds of virtual people under the pulsing lights, all dressed up to go out, dancing to a fastidiously curated soundtrack featuring some of the real world’s most famous artists as the controller pulses to the bassline in your hands. These big nights out are an opportunity for both Vice City’s sleaziest denizens and Rockstar’s developers to flash their cash: they are the game’s most ostentatiously expensive and showy scenarios. But at the centre of it all, there are Jason and Lucia, dancing together, focused on each other in the midst of all this chaos and excess. Keza is one of the first people to have played GTA VI. Ask her anything in our live Q&A at 4pm today. Join here . Grand Theft Auto VI is out 19 November; £69.99 / €79.99 / A$159.95 / $79.99

This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story, from up-and-coming rappers to Lucia’s mother, from a jaded strip-club worker to a badass middle-aged drug-runner whose custom purple carbine rifle is her prized possession. This is a game in which women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men. And without wanting to give too much away: there are male strippers in Leonida, too.

I am not about to make a case for GTA VI as a feminist game – there is much to be offended by here, if you are so inclined – but I will say that as a woman who has played and enjoyed every GTA game while also often rolling my eyes at their casual sniggering misogyny, GTA VI hits different for me. I liked it more because the women aren’t always the butt of a joke. Also for the first time, I did not find the violence gratuitous or overblown, despite the fact that this is a story about crime and criminals. There is nothing here like GTA V’s infamous torture mission , which made me feel sick. It says a lot that of all the immoral opportunities afforded to me in Vice City, the only thing I straight-up said “no” to was getting involved in a metaverse scam. THAT would be going too far.

I keep reaching for something that sums up GTA VI, as much as it’s possible to sum up a game as vast as this, and the closest I come is the nightclubs. These show GTA VI at its most extravagant: hundreds of virtual people under the pulsing lights, all dressed up to go out, dancing to a fastidiously curated soundtrack featuring some of the real world’s most famous artists as the controller pulses to the bassline in your hands. These big nights out are an opportunity for both Vice City’s sleaziest denizens and Rockstar’s developers to flash their cash: they are the game’s most ostentatiously expensive and showy scenarios. But at the centre of it all, there are Jason and Lucia, dancing together, focused on each other in the midst of all this chaos and excess.
Keza is one of the first people to have played GTA VI. Ask her anything in our live Q&A at 4pm today. Join here .
Grand Theft Auto VI is out 19 November; £69.99 / €79.99 / A$159.95 / $79.99

extraction.body: How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade. That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive. I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine. Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it. Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

passages: While it may seem impossible for anything in our universe to live up to the hype and anticipation Grand Theft Auto 6 has garnered, Rockstar has done the impossible.
GTA VI offers more in a single package than any video game before it, blowing past its status as one of the best action games of all time into one of the best life-sims of all time.
It may sound like hyperbole, but GTA VI is so chock full of content that it feels like several fully-fleshed out games in one.
It’s been so long since the (still incredible) GTA V launched that there are people who weren’t born at the time who are now teenagers (no, you’re not old enough to play yet, son, and go to bed!).
