extraction.body: Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers an enormous open world, a gripping story, a vibrant Vice City and an astonishing range of activities. If there’s one thing Rockstar can never be accused of, it’s rushing out Grand Theft Auto VI . It’s been so long since the (still incredible) GTA V launched that there are people who weren’t born at the time who are now teenagers (no, you’re not old enough to play yet, son, and go to bed!). It’s not like Rockstar wasn’t busy during that time — they’ve been constantly updating the ever-growing Grand Theft Auto Online and also happened to release one of the greatest westerns of all time in Red Dead Redemption II . Yet all of the many years of development somehow becomes immediately apparent the second you pass the title screen. Put simply, this is one of the largest and most ambitious games ever created. GTA 6 centers around the complicated personal and professional relationship of two criminals, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, and their journey through the realistically hard-to-succeed-in world of Vice City. That’s about the only story element I’m comfortable sharing, however, as this is a game that begs not to be spoiled and to be experienced as fresh as possible. From DMA Design to GTA III, GTA V, and RDR2, let's take a look back at how Rockstar Games changed open-world gaming and why GTA 6 has so much to live up to. While you can follow the main story all the way through, complete tons of side quests or simply take part in what the most depraved of us do and make the game into a rampage simulator, there are so many activities here that almost any one of them could be focused on as a full game. There’s diving for treasure, bird watching, fishing, customizing cars and oh so many other things that are fully fleshed out and not just throwaway afterthoughts. In fact, just existing in the game is so complex now that GTA has basically become a life sim. Upon awakening, you can eat, make coffee, watch TV, play video games, workout, watch a show, do home repairs, feed pets and enough other tasks to make a list of them as long as a full review. It’s incredibly cool for the world to feel so realistic that you literally sometimes get stressed out from knowing you have to do a chore and can’t just go run people down (I guess I am one of the depraved ones after all). Sometimes an hour is spent in GTA VI literally lifting weights, drinking a protein drink, grocery shopping and laying down in bed doomscrolling. While that might not exactly be the sentence to sell you on the game, the fact that GTA VI is just that deep and manages to make it all enjoyable to carry out truly speaks to the attention to detail at play. It goes beyond simply just blazing through the world doing horrible things and hoping a cop doesn’t see it — there are immediate and severe consequences to your actions now. That being said, it’s hard to criticize Rockstar for the game being too realistic, and once you adapt to its ebb and flow, this new realistic GTA experience feels all the more enveloping as it stimulates the anxiety, stress and fear synapses as much as the happiness ones, making successful accomplishments in the game all the more rewarding. It’s impossible to review GTA VI without touching on the music, and if I had my way, this entire review would just be speaking about that. But as I don’t want to risk you clicking out since we could really use those GTA page views, I’ll keep it short. The score itself is composed by famed French electronic duo, Justice, and is like an aural hug to the ears. The instrumentals during key action scenes are some of the best heard since HEALTH’s stunning Max Payne 3 score and get the adrenaline pumping. The included original songs Justice recorded are so expertly crafted to sound like ‘80s hits that I was literally googling the lyrics thinking I had found long lost ‘80s songs before realizing it was actually Justice. Considering I’m big Justice fan who’ve seen their live show multiple times, that says a lot that they even fooled me. Rockstar has released GTA 6’s launch trailer, spotlighting Jason and Lucia while confirming Justice as the composers of its original score. It’d be fair to judge a GTA by its radio stations as they play such an integral part in the experience and are heard for literally hundreds of hours by most players, so thankfully there’s another incredible lineup here. There’s a channel for everybody — ranging from buttrock to country to reggae to classical music to many, many more. Fans of past channels like Radio Broker and Radio Mirror Park will be happy to hear that there’s another hipster/indie style channel in GTA VI dubbed “ Stockyard FM ” which plays music from the likes of Hot Chip, Nation of Language, !!! and even debuts a new song from the aforementioned HEALTH. Flash FM quickly becomes a favorite as well, focusing on high energy dance pop and electro pop from artists like Billie Eilish, The Ting Tings and more. Finally, Circoloco Records is a commendable addition featuring smooth throwback-style electronic music from Rockstar ’s own record label. But expect to hear a fantastically curated soundtrack no matter which station you jam out to, with artists ranging anywhere from The Weeknd to Steve Winwood. With how many flawlessly-executed mechanics and elements to GTA 6 there is, it’s hard to find faults. There’s not even many glitches that occur, which is shocking for an open world game of the magnitude. Possibly the only criticism would be that it's so complex and ambitious that the learning curve is steep, and even after dozens of hours in the game, it’s easy to forget how a certain mechanic works or which button does what at times. Of course, criticizing something for being so deep proves difficult and at the very least perhaps a good problem to have in the end. Rockstar has minimized the complexity as much as they could by providing an easy-to-access control list at all times and basically devoting the first twenty or so hours of the story as a backdoor tutorial. Considering how enormous the scope of GTA 6 is, it’d be easy to forgive it for having visuals not up to snuff, yet it boasts some of the most realistic character models seen in gaming and uses them throughout all of the beautifully-choreographed in-game cutscenes. The way the characters are rendered give them a certain unique realistic element that has never quite been captured before — from unique body types to random skin marks to life behind the eyes. As good as the characters look, the environments might look even better with everything from trees to the pavement itself rich in detail. There’s also incredible lighting work at play that makes everything pop like you’d expect Florida, er, Vice City to. While it may seem impossible for anything in our universe to live up to the hype and anticipation Grand Theft Auto 6 has garnered, Rockstar has done the impossible. GTA VI offers more in a single package than any video game before it, blowing past its status as one of the best action games of all time into one of the best life-sims of all time. And one of the best driving games of all time. And one of the best…birding…games of all time? It may sound like hyperbole, but GTA VI is so chock full of content that it feels like several fully-fleshed out games in one. And that’s not to mention it actually does have several fully-fleshed out games within a game inside of it. GTA VI may not completely reinvent the wheel, but it fully commands it, delivering an enormous adventure that’s chock-full of enough things to keep you busy until Grand Theft Auto VII (please, Rockstar ?). The last thirteen years were more than worth the wait and make Grand Theft Auto VI go down as an unparalleled achievement in video games.

passages: For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite.
It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail.
It's about big ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals.
It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity.

Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part.
You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown.
Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else.
If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible.
These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance.
Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough.
The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point.
This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly.
Americans, they said, paraphrasing, have found a new 'third place': the car.
I know I said it's irreducible, but I can't help it.
For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money.

How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down.
At every tier of life savings, after every big score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again.
It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless.
These aren't the only things they're about, obviously.
But by virtue of being games depicting the world as it was in some way, they also become a reflection of it.

GTA 5 , its Los Santos-set predecessor, was aware enough of the importance of the car to name an in-game canyon after Reyner Banham, the British architectural critic who described Los Angeles' freeway system, one of the city's "four ecologies", as "Autopia".
For the longest time I really thought that idea summed up GTA 6 quite nicely.
Maybe it's a natural response to something too big and unwieldy to instantly get your head around: to seize the first acceptable idea and declare it just 'x' .
To admit something is too complex for you to immediately summarise is far less comfortable than simply dismissing it on the spot.
Who they're running from, or why they're being chased quite so hard, remains agonisingly beyond their field of view.

I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's.
Where you do much of your discovery of this properly, disorientatingly, astoundingly big and detailed world.
Where you'll be when you find the most 'emergent events'.

At first it might be via minor drug deals, collected and delivered via your boss' bi-plane, or discovering a small-time criminal operation to rob out the back of a local liquor store.
These are a rare example of Rockstar seemingly taking outside inspiration - criminal operations, marked on your map in yellow once discovered, are essentially Ubisoft-like outposts.
They're dense scenarios that essentially offer a more combat-focused route to money, and a texture-forward slice of the game's criminal world.
And those quieter aspects are a necessary foil - in fact, they're really a place where Rockstar exercises some rare subtlety.
In a way, it comes just as a real relationship does.

After a mission together with some classic, larger-than-life GTA character or other, they'll occasionally have a little debrief, in the way a real couple might the morning after a particularly lurid double-date.
They'll check-in, chit-chat, hang out, discuss hopes for the future, fears about what might happen, skepticism that they'll ever escape this constant whirlpool.
How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami".
Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn.
And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance.
And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff.
Lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L.
Perez - is astoundingly natural, charismatic, authentic in her delivery.
The range of this character takes her from fierce to afraid, giddy and giggly to imperiously strong, or petal soft.
And despite those extremes of emotion, and GTA characters' historic knack of scenery-chewing, she is never a caricature; between those two far ends lies the entire spectrum, too.
Next to the sheer dazzle of Lucia, you need a straight-man to play off.
And so where she might shine with sass, or protectiveness, or playful faux annoyance for a laugh, Jason might offer an eye roll, a sigh, or some other exasperation under his breath.
He's also - at least with the relationship at its strongest - a surprisingly fine example of the strong, yet thoroughly non-toxic man; gentle and considerate, reassuring and attentive.

extraction.body: My best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely. This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly. Americans, they said, paraphrasing, have found a new 'third place': the car. I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's. But here it felt just right: GTA 6 is, of course, a game both about America and about the personal vehicle. The clue's in the name. And as you play GTA 6, you realise, over and over, that the car is where so much of this game happens. It's where you take calls that lead to missions or story developments; where you pick up, hang out with, and chat to your partner; where you race away from police, gangs, wild animals and weirdos. Where you do much of your discovery of this properly, disorientatingly, astoundingly big and detailed world. Where you'll be when you find the most 'emergent events'. And, more than it's ever been before, the car is now an essential partner in itself; a place to stow weapons, disguises, and stolen goods - a companion it feels almost impossible to do without. I could go on about this. GTA 6 is a game of perpetual motion, as protagonists Jason and Lucia do their best to outrun a world that so often feels a step ahead - and which often culminates in some of the most exhilarating, astonishing chase sequences ever built in a video game. GTA 5 , its Los Santos-set predecessor, was aware enough of the importance of the car to name an in-game canyon after Reyner Banham, the British architectural critic who described Los Angeles' freeway system, one of the city's "four ecologies", as "Autopia". So yes: the car is the third place, in modern America and in GTA 6. The place of self-actualisation between work and home - two points that, for GTA 6's protagonists in particular, seem to always be in a state of flux. Maybe the car's their true home. For the longest time I really thought that idea summed up GTA 6 quite nicely. Until I didn't. Reducing GTA 6 to just the car, I realised, looking at it through only that one lens, forces you to be too narrow. You miss too much of it. What about the romance? The sensuality? The people and the natural world? And so what I've come to settle on instead - and honestly I expect this to change many more times over the coming days and weeks too, as even more of this horizonless game rolls back to reveal itself - is that GTA 6 just doesn't have a single thread to pull on. No one thing that, when properly grasped, suddenly draws it into a manageable shape. I've no doubt we'll all try. People have, for whatever reason, always reached for the most reductive ideas when they talk about Grand Theft Auto in particular. Maybe it's a natural response to something too big and unwieldy to instantly get your head around: to seize the first acceptable idea and declare it just 'x' . To admit something is too complex for you to immediately summarise is far less comfortable than simply dismissing it on the spot. Whatever it is, GTA 6 isn't just anything. For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite. It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail. It's about big ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals. It's ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar. It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity. Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part. You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown. Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else. If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible. None of that is to say it's perfect. It's easy to stand in front of something like this and just bask in the awe of it, forgetting to stop a moment and step back. The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome, but there are also nits to pick. But then you step back again and they tend to fade away. GTA 6 will not be for everyone. But no game has made a better attempt at being everything. GTA 6's story begins with Jason and Lucia. Discussing it beyond that is, frankly, almost impossible to do with any kind of substance without also spoiling it. For all the precipitous leaks, Rockstar has kept its story's two most essential moments - its beginning and its end - entirely secret, and without those two moments we're only really left with euphemisms. Jason and Lucia are on the run, after a seemingly simple fetch quest goes awry. Who they're running from, or why they're being chased quite so hard, remains agonisingly beyond their field of view. But what is clear, right from the off, is exactly why they're so determined to escape. And amongst all this Rockstar has achieved something kind of momentous, when it comes to Grand Theft Auto: we've got real and very human stakes. What else can be said? Well, let's go back to Rockstar's decision to begin so explicitly with Jason and Lucia. This is a story about a relationship. You can nurture or neglect it, but fundamentally that relationship - however strong - is at the heart of things. The fact that Grand Theft Auto 6, of all games, is in many ways a game about love, and arguably the first blockbuster video game to be quite so explicitly a love story, is notable enough on its own. These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance. Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough. But should I pick up some flowers first? The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point. Buying flowers, for instance, is one of the game's early, albeit optional missions. You begin GTA 6 proper playing solely as Jason for a short while, as he waits in his hazy, barefoot, margarita-soaked island hometown for Lucia to be released from prison. The two have been separated, their relationship effectively and conveniently reset - what kind of impression do you want to make when you finally see her after all this time? While the urge might be to test out those new wanted mechanics or - as recent memes would have it - race across the map to the first stripclub you can find, suddenly you have an altogether different to-do list. Back to Jason and Lucia. The other thought I kept returning to is how profound a bond I started to form with them. I have to admit: I've tended not to care much about video game characters, frankly. Even in the obvious games, where voice actors have started to attract almost cult-like followings, I've never really got it. The closest any game has got to making me cry is in Football Manager 23, when I lost the Champions League final in the dying minutes to PSG. But with Jason and Lucia, suddenly I think I get it. I put much of this down to the performances - they are spellbinding - but really it's all interconnected, a factor of the extreme levels of development craft, from animation to cutscene direction, and of several relatively simple, but smartly executed systems layered on top (more on those later). Lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L. Perez - is astoundingly natural, charismatic, authentic in her delivery. The range of this character takes her from fierce to afraid, giddy and giggly to imperiously strong, or petal soft. And despite those extremes of emotion, and GTA characters' historic knack of scenery-chewing, she is never a caricature; between those two far ends lies the entire spectrum, too. Jason, prosaic and inarticulate - arguably even shy - feels destined to be underappreciated by comparison, but there's something to his performance also. Next to the sheer dazzle of Lucia, you need a straight-man to play off. And so where she might shine with sass, or protectiveness, or playful faux annoyance for a laugh, Jason might offer an eye roll, a sigh, or some other exasperation under his breath. He's also - at least with the relationship at its strongest - a surprisingly fine example of the strong, yet thoroughly non-toxic man; gentle and considerate, reassuring and attentive. Occasionally I have to catch myself, before I start believing GTA 6 - again, of all games - might genuinely be the game to offer the most persuasive model of a positive relationship to the kids who play it. (Again, aside from all the killing and stuff). And those quieter aspects are a necessary foil - in fact, they're really a place where Rockstar exercises some rare subtlety. Some of GTA 6's funniest moments - between the big, obvious, admittedly still very funny gags for this childish mind (be sure to look out for all the game's many WAiNK locations!) - come from almost imperceptible glances and asides amongst the chaos. Together, both protagonists feel somewhat aware of the ludicrousness of the world around them, even more than they are simply a part of it.The two stars' relationship - and I chose to lean into this all the way, full 'wife guy' Jason and guard-down Lucia - is developed through minutiae. In a way, it comes just as a real relationship does. Little touches, side eyes, in jokes. After a mission together with some classic, larger-than-life GTA character or other, they'll occasionally have a little debrief, in the way a real couple might the morning after a particularly lurid double-date. They'll check-in, chit-chat, hang out, discuss hopes for the future, fears about what might happen, skepticism that they'll ever escape this constant whirlpool. And how you've behaved so far will dictate how the other might respond, with reassurance and commitment or something else. Small gestures will add up, and both parties have to contribute. You can hold hands whenever you're together, open car doors for each other, send check-in texts or invitations to hang out. But it gets even more menial than that. Sometimes it's just sitting on the sofa together, watching TV or talking about nothing in particular (on the topic of TV: GTA 6 has a number of fully fledged TV shows, from Weasel News to actual, fully realised cartoon animations with multiple episodes; it also has four fully playable video games, including a pastiche arthouse walking simulator and twin-stick extraction shooter). Other times, sure, it's a particular kind of passion ignited by the unique thrill of a violent, climactic mission. This couple can be a burning cocktail, if you want them to be, born of extreme external danger and the safety of each other's embrace. And in their most tender moments, handled with genuine attentiveness and sincerity, it's intoxicating. None of this, crucially, feels like a chore. Instead it feels almost irresistible, the easiest and most natural role play, created in part by Rockstar smartly prompting you with certain icons in moments, incentivising you with the tease of branching narrative - the idea in the back of your mind that there's some kind of outcome, somewhere in here, if things go a certain way. In others, they leave it to you: if I hadn't approached Lucia in the kitchen one early-game morning and pressed L2 to see what interactions came up, I wouldn't have noticed I had the option to offer her a lift to work, another little moment to bond. All together, it's a picture of what many great relationships - maybe minus the rampages - become as a whole. A series of grand memories made together, sure - across rooftop bars, helicopter rides, and sunsets at the beach, maybe a couple of bank robberies and killing sprees - but also hours upon hours of touches, jokes, hugs, nicknames, shared friends, cups of coffee, dancing, laughter, or long, quiet journeys in the car. It is without doubt the most believable, captivating relationship I've ever played. I could talk forever about this pair, not just in their relationship but as characters, extensions of GTA 6's thematic world. At various moments in my time with the game, for instance, I found myself wondering about Lucia's experience of the world, and how Rockstar uses its famously detestable NPCs - individually written and constructed in the thousands, another quietly stunning factor in this game - to occasionally play the role of, for instance, leering older men. How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami". Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn. And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance. And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff. How the two of them wrestle with their position of desperation, poverty and precariousness in the world of Leonida, a microcosm of Rockstar's take on the United States. I should probably start talking about that world. Where to begin? Let's start with the obvious stuff: GTA 6's map is absolutely massive. I haven't tested this directly, but the leaked maps are more or less accurate, and the comparisons in terms of size - multiple GTA 5's within GTA 6's map of Leonida - are about right. After dozens and dozens of hours with it there are still little areas, islands, and archipelagos I haven't explored, and many more spots so rarely visited they still feel entirely new when I drive through them again. Soon after that little diversion in the woods, up on the scraggy peak I'd originally set out to reach, a wave of fog rolled in, bringing visibility eerily close amongst colonial-era ruins, crumbling log cabins, and the rusted-out tracks of disused, Old West mine carts. Hikers strolled by with a nod. Then, a firewatch tower I'd sought to climb for a proper view offered me the start of one of several mysteries GTA 6 has laid out here for players, continuing the series' long-running tradition. Later that evening, after finding and raiding an encampment of drug runners, being chased, found, and chased again by police, nosing around a nudist colony, then an eerily romantic lover's lookout (plus another bizarre encounter I won't spoil), I drove my couple home, to the city in the south, country radio giving way to electronica, and thunderclouds rolled in, soaking the hills and fields and miles upon miles of tarmac as much with atmosphere as with the rain itself. Time and time again you'll find yourself in moments like this, not really doing anything or going anywhere - or suddenly abandoning plans for something stranger, more curious. But crucially still passing through the world, typically from the seat of a car. Right near the beginning of the game, in the first miniature moment of free roam with Jason - a short car journey home from wherever it was I was doing some fresh-from-prologue activity - I hit a perfect example of this. Rockstar clearly knows the value of the first drive: night, rain on the asphalt, Vice City FM on the radio, red tail lights flaring the lens. That's one I've never grown tired of, and probably never will: the tail lights. A kind of universal symbol of America's bigness, your tiny position in the queue of thousands, amongst this sea of snaking red stars against the darkness. All this together an absolutely superlative vibe. I expect everyone will find their own little fascination like this. All of these things come as a result of Rockstar's ludicrous budget and infinite runway, but also an obvious determination to use that almighty privilege to its fullest. This studio has always been emphatically, maybe fanatically focused on detail, and now it's had the greatest opportunity to exploit that obsession that might ever be afforded to a developer. And so detail is everywhere; from the way Jason's t-shirt creases as he walks or rumples in the wind, to the noise and gust kicked up by helicopters; hair that flows impossibly like water, water that actually looks like water, sweat on skin, and sweat on bottles , and dusted condensation on cars. One of the very first things I wrote down in my notes on this game, as Lucia paced the hallway of her prison, was about a patch of mismatched paint on the wall. Speaking of, let's get into some mechanics, where all these tension points are at their strongest. GTA 6 works like this: Jason and Lucia's story is spread over a prologue and then several chapters. The world is open more or less from the off, not dissimilar to GTA 5, and yet the game, to borrow a term from Rockstar, is "stratified" in how it gradually rolls out its systems and greatest rewards. In other words, there's a little bit of progression to get through before what feels like the true GTA 6 reveals itself. And the real drive here, insofar as there is one, is earning money. GTA 6 is easily the purest expression of life as an actual thief that Rockstar has attempted to make. Theft is at the heart and all along the spine of Jason and Lucia's story. From the setup of the game's prologue to the inciting incident its entire, lengthy first chapter builds to, and then well beyond it, all the way through to the finale. Over time, for instance, you'll have a perpetual optional objective: to top up your joint savings account to higher and higher targets, essentially building a flight fund or future life, whatever it may ultimately be. Likewise at various points you'll need to spend a certain amount of money with someone or on something to progress. And throughout, money is ultimately the gatekeeper to the game. Money is the "bridges" of previous GTAs, if you like: in the very early game you can, as far as I could tell, go more or less anywhere. But to actually do anything worthwhile and engage with Leonida's many, many activities, you'll need to both progress the story and get a bank account, the latter of which our dear off-the-grid, dishonourably-discharged minor criminal Jason has so far opted against. Over and over then, you'll find yourself scraping together cash, and gradually GTA 6 offers newer, more rewarding and more complex means of doing so. At first it might be via minor drug deals, collected and delivered via your boss' bi-plane, or discovering a small-time criminal operation to rob out the back of a local liquor store. Then it might be stealing some low-tier cars to flip to a new-found fence, or busting bigger drug operations and gang hideouts. These are a rare example of Rockstar seemingly taking outside inspiration - criminal operations, marked on your map in yellow once discovered, are essentially Ubisoft-like outposts. At first I wondered if that might be a drawback, but then separate the idea and execution itself from the stigma and I don't think so. They're dense scenarios that essentially offer a more combat-focused route to money, and a texture-forward slice of the game's criminal world. In the simplest terms they're also quite fun, and a nice break from all the other forms of theft. Theft continues beyond that still. You soon learn how to stick up minor stores and restaurants, and rob people at gunpoint on the street. Then it's pawn shops, jewellery stores, payday loan businesses. Then before you know it you're ripping ATMs out of walls with a tow truck, hurtling down the highway with this big metal cube still attached like a bouncing, sentient steel piñata on the run, until it cracks open for you to feast on its delicious insides. Then you're yoinking supercars or - and oh, this is the good stuff - robbing full-fledged banks at will. It's also uninvasive, I found, thanks to clearly marked, and relatively long, windows around maintaining your current status, but there's still a level of detail here. Your body composition is dictated by both cardio and strength training, but also what you eat and how often. You can ignore it and just look like an average person, or pay attention for meaningful buffs to health, focus, stamina, and appearance - and naturally the world around you reacts to that in comments from passers-by and, I suspect, small details of certain missions changing too. There's more! There's racing - at racetracks and mud tracks; in street races and off road courses; with bikes, cars, drones, and the rest. There are stunt jumps, naturally, and basejumps too. There are places to meditate. There's a system around not just fishing but using the right bait, multiple series of collectible trading cards to hoard or sell, various collectible books and magazines, meteorites, golden doubloons, and 'key valuables' found at gang hideouts including one-off guns, cars, and jewellery like fancy watches. There are clubs, bars, strippers, love hotels, diners, coffee houses, stores of clothing and shoes, hairdressers, and beyond. You can play an alarmingly realistic version of pool. Or listen to the radio of course - there are roughly double the stations you've seen revealed so far - or numerous talk shows and podcasts, including entire true crime dramas and series. You can ride jetskis, pose in rented supercars, order cocktails at swanky pools and go on dates to rooftop restaurants or crusty marina dive bars. There are DJs and live performances, including a cover band with the most accurately depicted, finger-specific fretting of a guitar solo I've ever seen in a game. The overall effect - yet another overall effect! I'm aware I keep doing this but I just have simply no other way of summarising it all - is of a genuine open-world playground, but crucially rather than a somewhat directionless soup of content, there is thematic sense to all of it. One of GTA 6's many messages, as foreshadowed on one of its most potent trailers, is a sense of embracing the moment while it lasts - of presentness and gratitude for things that might be accessible even without the big financial grind. And, surely, of what a joy it is to experience them with someone else. What else? Not much, frankly. On the technical side, I had one hard crash in my entire time with the game, which did cost me about 25 minutes of a mission, and one moment where an NPC got stuck trying to enter my car and I had to reload to a checkpoint made seconds earlier. I also wish there were more save slots - GTA 6 does away with mission replayability, which might prove controversial. As you play it you'll realise why that makes sense, but I also longed for more room than the 15 given to load back in at various moments and replay something specific - often for no other reason than that moment being an utter banger. Performance-wise, yes it plays at 30fps, even on a PS5 Pro , but Rockstar's frame pacing - I have to assume it's this; I'm no tech expert here - is so good that it feels resoundingly smoother than a typical game that runs at the same rate. Put aside the arbitrary number and ask me purely how it feels, and I'd tell you it feels smooth. How that fares on other consoles, particularly the Xbox Series S, will be worth considering. A little more philosophically, it's also not a perfect narrative, arguably because it never really could be. The middle of the game is phenomenal in its mission variety and excitement, though perhaps where Jason and Lucia's characters are pushed slightly to the background, when I wish their relationship - or lack of it - had even more time in the narrative spotlight. For all its dramatic heft, GTA 6 also can't purely be a drama, and so there is inevitably some tonal whiplash between an intimate love scene, say, and a quest involving chasing a man with a fake English accent wearing nothing but a comedy man thong around the poshest part of town. The point, instead, comes back to how all those strange and implausible bedfellows combine. And this is the magic. Every modern Grand Theft Auto is considered now to be a kind of product of its time. Nico Bellic's story is labelled a tale of the immigrant experience of the American Dream, amongst the post-9/11 world of New York and the war on terror. I always thought of GTA 5 as something prodding at a crisis of masculinity, after the financial crisis, and a kind of early 2010s complacency and drift. These aren't the only things they're about, obviously. GTA 5 is also The Sopranos and an ode to LA and the split of the id, ego, and superego, and of course a broad, hours-long, occasionally mis-targeted piss-take. But by virtue of being games depicting the world as it was in some way, they also become a reflection of it. What is Grand Theft Auto 6, then? I know I said it's irreducible, but I can't help it. For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money. How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down. At every tier of life savings, after every big score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again. It might be trite, but it feels essential to point out nonetheless, that GTA 6 is a product of capitalism at its most extreme: the most extraordinary amount of wealth ever directed at an entertainment product and, surely, the one to achieve the most extraordinary number of sales. It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless. GTA 6 is a reflection of the outer world and a part of it. And at its heart, its fragile and desperate humans play a rigged game, while attempting to walk the narrow line between exhausted desperation and the empowering wish-fulfilment of crime. You might wonder, as Jason and Lucia often do, whether they're always going to be doomed. And then later, whether that matters, when the beauty of it all is in the struggle.
passages: My best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely. This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly. Americans, they said, paraphrasing, have found a new 'third place': the car.

I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's. But here it felt just right: GTA 6 is, of course, a game both about America and about the personal vehicle. The clue's in the name. And as you play GTA 6, you realise, over and over, that the car is where so much of this game happens. It's where you take calls that lead to missions or story developments; where you pick up, hang out with, and chat to your partner; where you race away from police, gangs, wild animals and weirdos. Where you do much of your discovery of this properly, disorientatingly, astoundingly big and detailed world. Where you'll be when you find the most 'emergent events'. And, more than it's ever been before, the car is now an essential partner in itself; a place to stow weapons, disguises, and stolen goods - a companion it feels almost impossible to do without.

I could go on about this. GTA 6 is a game of perpetual motion, as protagonists Jason and Lucia do their best to outrun a world that so often feels a step ahead - and which often culminates in some of the most exhilarating, astonishing chase sequences ever built in a video game. GTA 5 , its Los Santos-set predecessor, was aware enough of the importance of the car to name an in-game canyon after Reyner Banham, the British architectural critic who described Los Angeles' freeway system, one of the city's "four ecologies", as "Autopia". So yes: the car is the third place, in modern America and in GTA 6. The place of self-actualisation between work and home - two points that, for GTA 6's protagonists in particular, seem to always be in a state of flux. Maybe the car's their true home. For the longest time I really thought that idea summed up GTA 6 quite nicely. Until I didn't.

Reducing GTA 6 to just the car, I realised, looking at it through only that one lens, forces you to be too narrow. You miss too much of it. What about the romance? The sensuality? The people and the natural world? And so what I've come to settle on instead - and honestly I expect this to change many more times over the coming days and weeks too, as even more of this horizonless game rolls back to reveal itself - is that GTA 6 just doesn't have a single thread to pull on. No one thing that, when properly grasped, suddenly draws it into a manageable shape.

I've no doubt we'll all try. People have, for whatever reason, always reached for the most reductive ideas when they talk about Grand Theft Auto in particular. Maybe it's a natural response to something too big and unwieldy to instantly get your head around: to seize the first acceptable idea and declare it just 'x' . To admit something is too complex for you to immediately summarise is far less comfortable than simply dismissing it on the spot.

Whatever it is, GTA 6 isn't just anything. For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite. It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail. It's about big ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals. It's ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar. It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity. Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part. You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown. Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else. If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible.

None of that is to say it's perfect. It's easy to stand in front of something like this and just bask in the awe of it, forgetting to stop a moment and step back. The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome, but there are also nits to pick. But then you step back again and they tend to fade away. GTA 6 will not be for everyone. But no game has made a better attempt at being everything.

GTA 6's story begins with Jason and Lucia. Discussing it beyond that is, frankly, almost impossible to do with any kind of substance without also spoiling it. For all the precipitous leaks, Rockstar has kept its story's two most essential moments - its beginning and its end - entirely secret, and without those two moments we're only really left with euphemisms.

Jason and Lucia are on the run, after a seemingly simple fetch quest goes awry. Who they're running from, or why they're being chased quite so hard, remains agonisingly beyond their field of view. But what is clear, right from the off, is exactly why they're so determined to escape. And amongst all this Rockstar has achieved something kind of momentous, when it comes to Grand Theft Auto: we've got real and very human stakes.

What else can be said? Well, let's go back to Rockstar's decision to begin so explicitly with Jason and Lucia. This is a story about a relationship. You can nurture or neglect it, but fundamentally that relationship - however strong - is at the heart of things.

The fact that Grand Theft Auto 6, of all games, is in many ways a game about love, and arguably the first blockbuster video game to be quite so explicitly a love story, is notable enough on its own. These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance. Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough. But should I pick up some flowers first? The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point.

Buying flowers, for instance, is one of the game's early, albeit optional missions. You begin GTA 6 proper playing solely as Jason for a short while, as he waits in his hazy, barefoot, margarita-soaked island hometown for Lucia to be released from prison. The two have been separated, their relationship effectively and conveniently reset - what kind of impression do you want to make when you finally see her after all this time? While the urge might be to test out those new wanted mechanics or - as recent memes would have it - race across the map to the first stripclub you can find, suddenly you have an altogether different to-do list.

Back to Jason and Lucia. The other thought I kept returning to is how profound a bond I started to form with them. I have to admit: I've tended not to care much about video game characters, frankly. Even in the obvious games, where voice actors have started to attract almost cult-like followings, I've never really got it. The closest any game has got to making me cry is in Football Manager 23, when I lost the Champions League final in the dying minutes to PSG. But with Jason and Lucia, suddenly I think I get it. I put much of this down to the performances - they are spellbinding - but really it's all interconnected, a factor of the extreme levels of development craft, from animation to cutscene direction, and of several relatively simple, but smartly executed systems layered on top (more on those later).

Lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L. Perez - is astoundingly natural, charismatic, authentic in her delivery. The range of this character takes her from fierce to afraid, giddy and giggly to imperiously strong, or petal soft. And despite those extremes of emotion, and GTA characters' historic knack of scenery-chewing, she is never a caricature; between those two far ends lies the entire spectrum, too. Jason, prosaic and inarticulate - arguably even shy - feels destined to be underappreciated by comparison, but there's something to his performance also. Next to the sheer dazzle of Lucia, you need a straight-man to play off. And so where she might shine with sass, or protectiveness, or playful faux annoyance for a laugh, Jason might offer an eye roll, a sigh, or some other exasperation under his breath. He's also - at least with the relationship at its strongest - a surprisingly fine example of the strong, yet thoroughly non-toxic man; gentle and considerate, reassuring and attentive. Occasionally I have to catch myself, before I start believing GTA 6 - again, of all games - might genuinely be the game to offer the most persuasive model of a positive relationship to the kids who play it. (Again, aside from all the killing and stuff).

And those quieter aspects are a necessary foil - in fact, they're really a place where Rockstar exercises some rare subtlety. Some of GTA 6's funniest moments - between the big, obvious, admittedly still very funny gags for this childish mind (be sure to look out for all the game's many WAiNK locations!) - come from almost imperceptible glances and asides amongst the chaos. Together, both protagonists feel somewhat aware of the ludicrousness of the world around them, even more than they are simply a part of it.The two stars' relationship - and I chose to lean into this all the way, full 'wife guy' Jason and guard-down Lucia - is developed through minutiae. In a way, it comes just as a real relationship does. Little touches, side eyes, in jokes. After a mission together with some classic, larger-than-life GTA character or other, they'll occasionally have a little debrief, in the way a real couple might the morning after a particularly lurid double-date. They'll check-in, chit-chat, hang out, discuss hopes for the future, fears about what might happen, skepticism that they'll ever escape this constant whirlpool. And how you've behaved so far will dictate how the other might respond, with reassurance and commitment or something else.

Small gestures will add up, and both parties have to contribute. You can hold hands whenever you're together, open car doors for each other, send check-in texts or invitations to hang out. But it gets even more menial than that. Sometimes it's just sitting on the sofa together, watching TV or talking about nothing in particular (on the topic of TV: GTA 6 has a number of fully fledged TV shows, from Weasel News to actual, fully realised cartoon animations with multiple episodes; it also has four fully playable video games, including a pastiche arthouse walking simulator and twin-stick extraction shooter). Other times, sure, it's a particular kind of passion ignited by the unique thrill of a violent, climactic mission. This couple can be a burning cocktail, if you want them to be, born of extreme external danger and the safety of each other's embrace. And in their most tender moments, handled with genuine attentiveness and sincerity, it's intoxicating.

None of this, crucially, feels like a chore. Instead it feels almost irresistible, the easiest and most natural role play, created in part by Rockstar smartly prompting you with certain icons in moments, incentivising you with the tease of branching narrative - the idea in the back of your mind that there's some kind of outcome, somewhere in here, if things go a certain way. In others, they leave it to you: if I hadn't approached Lucia in the kitchen one early-game morning and pressed L2 to see what interactions came up, I wouldn't have noticed I had the option to offer her a lift to work, another little moment to bond.

All together, it's a picture of what many great relationships - maybe minus the rampages - become as a whole. A series of grand memories made together, sure - across rooftop bars, helicopter rides, and sunsets at the beach, maybe a couple of bank robberies and killing sprees - but also hours upon hours of touches, jokes, hugs, nicknames, shared friends, cups of coffee, dancing, laughter, or long, quiet journeys in the car. It is without doubt the most believable, captivating relationship I've ever played.

I could talk forever about this pair, not just in their relationship but as characters, extensions of GTA 6's thematic world. At various moments in my time with the game, for instance, I found myself wondering about Lucia's experience of the world, and how Rockstar uses its famously detestable NPCs - individually written and constructed in the thousands, another quietly stunning factor in this game - to occasionally play the role of, for instance, leering older men. How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami". Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn. And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance. And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff. How the two of them wrestle with their position of desperation, poverty and precariousness in the world of Leonida, a microcosm of Rockstar's take on the United States.

I should probably start talking about that world. Where to begin? Let's start with the obvious stuff: GTA 6's map is absolutely massive. I haven't tested this directly, but the leaked maps are more or less accurate, and the comparisons in terms of size - multiple GTA 5's within GTA 6's map of Leonida - are about right. After dozens and dozens of hours with it there are still little areas, islands, and archipelagos I haven't explored, and many more spots so rarely visited they still feel entirely new when I drive through them again.

Soon after that little diversion in the woods, up on the scraggy peak I'd originally set out to reach, a wave of fog rolled in, bringing visibility eerily close amongst colonial-era ruins, crumbling log cabins, and the rusted-out tracks of disused, Old West mine carts. Hikers strolled by with a nod. Then, a firewatch tower I'd sought to climb for a proper view offered me the start of one of several mysteries GTA 6 has laid out here for players, continuing the series' long-running tradition. Later that evening, after finding and raiding an encampment of drug runners, being chased, found, and chased again by police, nosing around a nudist colony, then an eerily romantic lover's lookout (plus another bizarre encounter I won't spoil), I drove my couple home, to the city in the south, country radio giving way to electronica, and thunderclouds rolled in, soaking the hills and fields and miles upon miles of tarmac as much with atmosphere as with the rain itself.

Time and time again you'll find yourself in moments like this, not really doing anything or going anywhere - or suddenly abandoning plans for something stranger, more curious. But crucially still passing through the world, typically from the seat of a car. Right near the beginning of the game, in the first miniature moment of free roam with Jason - a short car journey home from wherever it was I was doing some fresh-from-prologue activity - I hit a perfect example of this. Rockstar clearly knows the value of the first drive: night, rain on the asphalt, Vice City FM on the radio, red tail lights flaring the lens. That's one I've never grown tired of, and probably never will: the tail lights. A kind of universal symbol of America's bigness, your tiny position in the queue of thousands, amongst this sea of snaking red stars against the darkness. All this together an absolutely superlative vibe.

I expect everyone will find their own little fascination like this. All of these things come as a result of Rockstar's ludicrous budget and infinite runway, but also an obvious determination to use that almighty privilege to its fullest. This studio has always been emphatically, maybe fanatically focused on detail, and now it's had the greatest opportunity to exploit that obsession that might ever be afforded to a developer. And so detail is everywhere; from the way Jason's t-shirt creases as he walks or rumples in the wind, to the noise and gust kicked up by helicopters; hair that flows impossibly like water, water that actually looks like water, sweat on skin, and sweat on bottles , and dusted condensation on cars. One of the very first things I wrote down in my notes on this game, as Lucia paced the hallway of her prison, was about a patch of mismatched paint on the wall.

Speaking of, let's get into some mechanics, where all these tension points are at their strongest. GTA 6 works like this: Jason and Lucia's story is spread over a prologue and then several chapters. The world is open more or less from the off, not dissimilar to GTA 5, and yet the game, to borrow a term from Rockstar, is "stratified" in how it gradually rolls out its systems and greatest rewards. In other words, there's a little bit of progression to get through before what feels like the true GTA 6 reveals itself.

And the real drive here, insofar as there is one, is earning money. GTA 6 is easily the purest expression of life as an actual thief that Rockstar has attempted to make. Theft is at the heart and all along the spine of Jason and Lucia's story. From the setup of the game's prologue to the inciting incident its entire, lengthy first chapter builds to, and then well beyond it, all the way through to the finale. Over time, for instance, you'll have a perpetual optional objective: to top up your joint savings account to higher and higher targets, essentially building a flight fund or future life, whatever it may ultimately be. Likewise at various points you'll need to spend a certain amount of money with someone or on something to progress. And throughout, money is ultimately the gatekeeper to the game. Money is the "bridges" of previous GTAs, if you like: in the very early game you can, as far as I could tell, go more or less anywhere. But to actually do anything worthwhile and engage with Leonida's many, many activities, you'll need to both progress the story and get a bank account, the latter of which our dear off-the-grid, dishonourably-discharged minor criminal Jason has so far opted against.

Over and over then, you'll find yourself scraping together cash, and gradually GTA 6 offers newer, more rewarding and more complex means of doing so. At first it might be via minor drug deals, collected and delivered via your boss' bi-plane, or discovering a small-time criminal operation to rob out the back of a local liquor store. Then it might be stealing some low-tier cars to flip to a new-found fence, or busting bigger drug operations and gang hideouts. These are a rare example of Rockstar seemingly taking outside inspiration - criminal operations, marked on your map in yellow once discovered, are essentially Ubisoft-like outposts. At first I wondered if that might be a drawback, but then separate the idea and execution itself from the stigma and I don't think so. They're dense scenarios that essentially offer a more combat-focused route to money, and a texture-forward slice of the game's criminal world. In the simplest terms they're also quite fun, and a nice break from all the other forms of theft.

Theft continues beyond that still. You soon learn how to stick up minor stores and restaurants, and rob people at gunpoint on the street. Then it's pawn shops, jewellery stores, payday loan businesses. Then before you know it you're ripping ATMs out of walls with a tow truck, hurtling down the highway with this big metal cube still attached like a bouncing, sentient steel piñata on the run, until it cracks open for you to feast on its delicious insides. Then you're yoinking supercars or - and oh, this is the good stuff - robbing full-fledged banks at will.

It's also uninvasive, I found, thanks to clearly marked, and relatively long, windows around maintaining your current status, but there's still a level of detail here. Your body composition is dictated by both cardio and strength training, but also what you eat and how often. You can ignore it and just look like an average person, or pay attention for meaningful buffs to health, focus, stamina, and appearance - and naturally the world around you reacts to that in comments from passers-by and, I suspect, small details of certain missions changing too.

There's more! There's racing - at racetracks and mud tracks; in street races and off road courses; with bikes, cars, drones, and the rest. There are stunt jumps, naturally, and basejumps too. There are places to meditate. There's a system around not just fishing but using the right bait, multiple series of collectible trading cards to hoard or sell, various collectible books and magazines, meteorites, golden doubloons, and 'key valuables' found at gang hideouts including one-off guns, cars, and jewellery like fancy watches. There are clubs, bars, strippers, love hotels, diners, coffee houses, stores of clothing and shoes, hairdressers, and beyond. You can play an alarmingly realistic version of pool. Or listen to the radio of course - there are roughly double the stations you've seen revealed so far - or numerous talk shows and podcasts, including entire true crime dramas and series. You can ride jetskis, pose in rented supercars, order cocktails at swanky pools and go on dates to rooftop restaurants or crusty marina dive bars. There are DJs and live performances, including a cover band with the most accurately depicted, finger-specific fretting of a guitar solo I've ever seen in a game.

The overall effect - yet another overall effect! I'm aware I keep doing this but I just have simply no other way of summarising it all - is of a genuine open-world playground, but crucially rather than a somewhat directionless soup of content, there is thematic sense to all of it. One of GTA 6's many messages, as foreshadowed on one of its most potent trailers, is a sense of embracing the moment while it lasts - of presentness and gratitude for things that might be accessible even without the big financial grind. And, surely, of what a joy it is to experience them with someone else.

What else? Not much, frankly. On the technical side, I had one hard crash in my entire time with the game, which did cost me about 25 minutes of a mission, and one moment where an NPC got stuck trying to enter my car and I had to reload to a checkpoint made seconds earlier.

I also wish there were more save slots - GTA 6 does away with mission replayability, which might prove controversial. As you play it you'll realise why that makes sense, but I also longed for more room than the 15 given to load back in at various moments and replay something specific - often for no other reason than that moment being an utter banger. Performance-wise, yes it plays at 30fps, even on a PS5 Pro , but Rockstar's frame pacing - I have to assume it's this; I'm no tech expert here - is so good that it feels resoundingly smoother than a typical game that runs at the same rate. Put aside the arbitrary number and ask me purely how it feels, and I'd tell you it feels smooth. How that fares on other consoles, particularly the Xbox Series S, will be worth considering.

A little more philosophically, it's also not a perfect narrative, arguably because it never really could be. The middle of the game is phenomenal in its mission variety and excitement, though perhaps where Jason and Lucia's characters are pushed slightly to the background, when I wish their relationship - or lack of it - had even more time in the narrative spotlight. For all its dramatic heft, GTA 6 also can't purely be a drama, and so there is inevitably some tonal whiplash between an intimate love scene, say, and a quest involving chasing a man with a fake English accent wearing nothing but a comedy man thong around the poshest part of town. The point, instead, comes back to how all those strange and implausible bedfellows combine.

And this is the magic. Every modern Grand Theft Auto is considered now to be a kind of product of its time. Nico Bellic's story is labelled a tale of the immigrant experience of the American Dream, amongst the post-9/11 world of New York and the war on terror. I always thought of GTA 5 as something prodding at a crisis of masculinity, after the financial crisis, and a kind of early 2010s complacency and drift. These aren't the only things they're about, obviously. GTA 5 is also The Sopranos and an ode to LA and the split of the id, ego, and superego, and of course a broad, hours-long, occasionally mis-targeted piss-take. But by virtue of being games depicting the world as it was in some way, they also become a reflection of it.

What is Grand Theft Auto 6, then? I know I said it's irreducible, but I can't help it. For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money. How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down. At every tier of life savings, after every big score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again. It might be trite, but it feels essential to point out nonetheless, that GTA 6 is a product of capitalism at its most extreme: the most extraordinary amount of wealth ever directed at an entertainment product and, surely, the one to achieve the most extraordinary number of sales. It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless.

GTA 6 is a reflection of the outer world and a part of it. And at its heart, its fragile and desperate humans play a rigged game, while attempting to walk the narrow line between exhausted desperation and the empowering wish-fulfilment of crime. You might wonder, as Jason and Lucia often do, whether they're always going to be doomed. And then later, whether that matters, when the beauty of it all is in the struggle.

The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.
While it may seem impossible for anything in our universe to live up to the hype and anticipation Grand Theft Auto 6 has garnered, Rockstar has done the impossible.
GTA VI offers more in a single package than any video game before it, blowing past its status as one of the best action games of all time into one of the best life-sims of all time.
It may sound like hyperbole, but GTA VI is so chock full of content that it feels like several fully-fleshed out games in one.
It’s been so long since the (still incredible) GTA V launched that there are people who weren’t born at the time who are now teenagers (no, you’re not old enough to play yet, son, and go to bed!).
For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite.
It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail.
It's about big ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals.
It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity.

Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part.
You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown.
Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else.
If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible.
These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance.
Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough.
The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point.
This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly.
Americans, they said, paraphrasing, have found a new 'third place': the car.
I know I said it's irreducible, but I can't help it.
For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money.

How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down.
At every tier of life savings, after every big score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again.
It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless.

How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami".
Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn.
And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance.
And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff.
Lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L.
