The flaw sits in the optimized Base64 decoder that the HotSpot JVM uses on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support. Oracle and OpenJDK have released patches, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged immediate patching . At time of writing on November 18 there has been no evidence found of in-the-wild exploitation of this bug.

Java4Shell is significant because Base64 decoding is routine in server software. Authentication headers, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertions, file uploads and API fields are all Base64 encoded, so internet-facing login and API services decode attacker-controlled data by design. Calif , the security firm that first reported the flaw, published a standalone trigger and said product-specific exploit chains would be held back until upgrades are more widespread. Details about the flaw became public before patches were available.

The store mask used by the decoder is wrong when the Base64 input ends in padding. As a result, the calculated output length underflows, and the decoder writes a full 64 bytes into a buffer that is smaller than that. According to Calif, a 65-byte input overflows the heap by 62 bytes, which corrupts adjacent Java objects, allowing an actor to gain heap read and write primitives, which makes the bug remotely exploitable.

Exploitation of the heap overflow depends on the layout of the target application, and a failed attempt can crash the JVM. A crash would result in denial of service, but Calif reported that retries often succeed. Heap memory disclosure is also possible. A client-side variant exists: a Java application that connects over Transport Layer Security (TLS) to a malicious server can be compromised.

Affected versions are OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (including 17.0.6 to 17.0.21), Java 21 before 21.0.13.1, Java 25 before 25.0.5.1 and Java 27. Oracle also lists Java SE 8 8u511b33-perf. Builds from Oracle, Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat and GraalVM are affected. Hosts must also run on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Ice Lake and newer and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Java 11, standard OpenJDK 8, ARM64 hosts and x86 processors without AVX-512 VBMI are not affected.

Enterprise and server deployments carry the most risk, particularly identity, application lifecycle, build pipeline, artifact and data platforms. Popular Java-based applications such as Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, Kafka and Elasticsearch could be affected. Many of these products ship their own bundled Java runtime, so organizations should check each vendor for updated releases and should not rely on the host's Java version alone. Consumers are mainly exposed through Java client applications.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of November 18, 2026. However, Calif published a trigger that reproduces the overflow. It also showed pre-authentication RCE in Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory and PingFederate, as well as post-authentication RCE in Apache Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Fake proof-of-concept repositories are likely to appear, and unpatched internet-facing Java services on AVX-512 hardware should be treated as potentially exposed.

A running JVM keeps the vulnerable code until it is restarted, so every Java process must be restarted after upgrading. Containers should be rebuilt on patched base images. coreStoryFacts.text: Nicknamed “Java4Shell” by Calif, the company whose researchers found it, CVE-2026-114938 was fixed by Oracle and the OpenJDK project on Tuesday.
Just patch as you normally do later on today – as you should have last month as there was a different unauth RCE vuln then,” he advised .

Caitlin Condon, VP of Security Research at VulnCheck, said that the company’s research team determined that exploitation is hardware-specific: “The vulnerable code runs only on CPUs that provide the AVX-512 VBMI (and BW) instruction features; CPUs without them fall back to a different decode path that does not contain the defect, so the vulnerable instructions don’t execute there.”
Despite Java4Shell’s current high profile, many security researchers pointed out that exploiting it for RCE is not easy and hinges on specific CPU, JDK, and Base64 prerequisites.
There is currently no evidence of successful attacks leveraging the flaw, but the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) “strongly urges” organizations to patch immediately.
“With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution.
VulnCheck doesn’t expect widespread exploitation, but expects narrow paths to RCE in specific applications. watchTowr likewise doesn’t expect the exploitation to be indiscriminate.
Oracle has rated the flaw 8.1 on CVSS 3.1, citing high attack complexity, while Calif gave it a 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

A critical vulnerability dubbed Java4Shell in OpenJDK, the open-source implementation of Java, can allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on popular enterprise applications, including Jenkins, Atlassian Jira, Confluence, and Keycloak.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , is a memory-corruption flaw in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding functionality that can be exploited to disclose sensitive information from memory or achieve remote code execution (RCE).
Java is one of the most widely used programming platforms in the world, powering enterprise applications, web services, financial systems, and critical business infrastructure.

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, as well as Java distributions built from the affected code, including Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, and Red Hat OpenJDK.
Over 1,000 GitLab servers vulnerable to ongoing RCE attacks
Because many applications use the same Java runtime, vulnerabilities in its core components can affect a wide range of different and unrelated applications.
Security researchers at Calif, who disclosed the flaw on Tuesday, rated it critical with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, while Oracle assigned it a lower severity rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1.
Alternatively, administrators running Java on x86-64 systems can use -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512 instructions.
However, these workarounds are temporary mitigations, and all developers should update the Java runtimes to the latest version.

However, the researchers said Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, and attackers must find an application-dependent way to deliver malicious Base64 data to the vulnerable decoder to achieve code execution.
Calif was also able to exploit the flaw in sample applications built using the Apache Struts and Spring Boot frameworks.

"This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as ' Java4Shell ,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK)," CISA said .
"Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution."

As reported previously by The Hacker News, Java4Shell can enable attackers without an account to execute arbitrary code on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, under default settings.

"If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access," CISA said.
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged organizations to immediately patch a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Oracle Java.

Calif , the security firm that first reported the flaw, published a standalone trigger and said product-specific exploit chains would be held back until upgrades are more widespread.
Details about the flaw became public before patches were available.
Symantec and Carbon Black Security Response is investigating this vulnerability, guidance and reproduction steps.
Full protection information is in the Symantec Protection Bulletin for Java4Shell .
The bulletin will be updated continuously as new information becomes available.

extraction.body: CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption flaw in Open Java Development Kit’s Base64 decoder, can allow unauthenticated attackers to run code on servers hosting widely used Java applications. Nicknamed “Java4Shell” by Calif, the company whose researchers found it, CVE-2026-114938 was fixed by Oracle and the OpenJDK project on Tuesday. There is currently no evidence of successful attacks leveraging the flaw, but the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) “strongly urges” organizations to patch immediately. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory,” Calif researchers explained . “With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =. In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by =.” SentinelOne noted that exploit traffic is specific to each application. “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words.” Calif researchers say they achieved unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) in default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. In Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, they managed RCE after authentication. “We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested,” they added , and said that security researcher samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with them. Oracle has rated the flaw 8.1 on CVSS 3.1, citing high attack complexity, while Calif gave it a 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. Despite Java4Shell’s current high profile, many security researchers pointed out that exploiting it for RCE is not easy and hinges on specific CPU, JDK, and Base64 prerequisites. Caitlin Condon, VP of Security Research at VulnCheck, said that the company’s research team determined that exploitation is hardware-specific: “The vulnerable code runs only on CPUs that provide the AVX-512 VBMI (and BW) instruction features; CPUs without them fall back to a different decode path that does not contain the defect, so the vulnerable instructions don’t execute there.” Crashing an affected JVM is trivial, VulnCheck found, and repeated requests can keep a service down. Achieving RCE, though, requires heap grooming and a separate memory leak to bypass address space layout randomization (ASLR). ARM64 CPUs are not affected, Calif researchers noted. According to Oracle, CVE-2026-114938 affects Oracle Java SE versions 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3 (and likely earlier), as well as Oracle GraalVM for JDK (versions 17.0.21.0.3 and 21.0.13.0.3) and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition (v21.3.20.0.3). Calif says that a number of Java distributions built on vulnerable OpenJDK versions are also affected: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, SAP SapMachine, BellSoft Liberica, and Red Hat OpenJDK. Fixed builds are getting released by the vendors and should be used. VulnCheck doesn’t expect widespread exploitation, but expects narrow paths to RCE in specific applications. watchTowr likewise doesn’t expect the exploitation to be indiscriminate. Calif has published a proof-of-concept that only checks whether a given JDK and CPU combination reproduces the memory corruption, and is holding back its product-specific exploit chains to give organizations time to upgrade. Still, they said that if took them just two hours and some AI help to create the first working exploit, and attackers can do the same (albeit more slowly). But there’s no need to panic, according to security researcher Kevin Beaumont. “[CVE-2026-114938] is not world ending. Just patch as you normally do later on today – as you should have last month as there was a different unauth RCE vuln then,” he advised . CISA advises organizations to review their software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, pinpoint affected installations, and apply relevant Java and vendor patches when they become available. “If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access,” the agency said , and urged organizations to monitor for suspicious activity (e.g., rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes).

passages: A critical vulnerability dubbed Java4Shell in OpenJDK, the open-source implementation of Java, can allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on popular enterprise applications, including Jenkins, Atlassian Jira, Confluence, and Keycloak.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , is a memory-corruption flaw in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding functionality that can be exploited to disclose sensitive information from memory or achieve remote code execution (RCE).
Java is one of the most widely used programming platforms in the world, powering enterprise applications, web services, financial systems, and critical business infrastructure.

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, as well as Java distributions built from the affected code, including Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, and Red Hat OpenJDK.

Because many applications use the same Java runtime, vulnerabilities in its core components can affect a wide range of different and unrelated applications.
Security researchers at Calif, who disclosed the flaw on Tuesday, rated it critical with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, while Oracle assigned it a lower severity rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1.
Alternatively, administrators running Java on x86-64 systems can use -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512 instructions.
However, these workarounds are temporary mitigations, and all developers should update the Java runtimes to the latest version.

However, the researchers said Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, and attackers must find an application-dependent way to deliver malicious Base64 data to the vulnerable decoder to achieve code execution.
Calif was also able to exploit the flaw in sample applications built using the Apache Struts and Spring Boot frameworks.
Calif says researcher Quang Luong discovered the flaw using OpenAI's Codex AI coding assistant, which helped identify the vulnerability during an audit of OpenJDK's internals.

extraction.body: A critical vulnerability in OpenJDK, CVE-2026-114938 (aka Java4Shell), was disclosed on November 17, 2026. The flaw sits in the optimized Base64 decoder that the HotSpot JVM uses on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support. Oracle and OpenJDK have released patches, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged immediate patching . At time of writing on November 18 there has been no evidence found of in-the-wild exploitation of this bug. Java4Shell is significant because Base64 decoding is routine in server software. Authentication headers, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertions, file uploads and API fields are all Base64 encoded, so internet-facing login and API services decode attacker-controlled data by design. Calif , the security firm that first reported the flaw, published a standalone trigger and said product-specific exploit chains would be held back until upgrades are more widespread. Details about the flaw became public before patches were available. The store mask used by the decoder is wrong when the Base64 input ends in padding. As a result, the calculated output length underflows, and the decoder writes a full 64 bytes into a buffer that is smaller than that. According to Calif, a 65-byte input overflows the heap by 62 bytes, which corrupts adjacent Java objects, allowing an actor to gain heap read and write primitives, which makes the bug remotely exploitable. Exploitation of the heap overflow depends on the layout of the target application, and a failed attempt can crash the JVM. A crash would result in denial of service, but Calif reported that retries often succeed. Heap memory disclosure is also possible. A client-side variant exists: a Java application that connects over Transport Layer Security (TLS) to a malicious server can be compromised. Affected versions are OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (including 17.0.6 to 17.0.21), Java 21 before 21.0.13.1, Java 25 before 25.0.5.1 and Java 27. Oracle also lists Java SE 8 8u511b33-perf. Builds from Oracle, Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat and GraalVM are affected. Hosts must also run on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Ice Lake and newer and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Java 11, standard OpenJDK 8, ARM64 hosts and x86 processors without AVX-512 VBMI are not affected. Enterprise and server deployments carry the most risk, particularly identity, application lifecycle, build pipeline, artifact and data platforms. Popular Java-based applications such as Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, Kafka and Elasticsearch could be affected. Many of these products ship their own bundled Java runtime, so organizations should check each vendor for updated releases and should not rely on the host's Java version alone. Consumers are mainly exposed through Java client applications. No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of November 18, 2026. However, Calif published a trigger that reproduces the overflow. It also showed pre-authentication RCE in Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory and PingFederate, as well as post-authentication RCE in Apache Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Fake proof-of-concept repositories are likely to appear, and unpatched internet-facing Java services on AVX-512 hardware should be treated as potentially exposed. Oracle released fixes in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update , alongside an OpenJDK advisory of the same date. Fixed builds are: A running JVM keeps the vulnerable code until it is restarted, so every Java process must be restarted after upgrading. Containers should be rebuilt on patched base images. Downstream vendors are rolling out their own fixes, and fixed builds for several of them were not yet published at time of writing. CISA also advised identifying all Java installations, including those bundled in third-party applications, containers and appliances, and prioritizing internet-facing systems. Where patching is not immediately possible, Calif lists two JVM options. Both require a restart and neither replaces patching. CISA also recommended compensating controls such as validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Defenders can look for Base64 tokens that contain an equals sign and whose length is not a multiple of four, decoder exceptions such as “Input byte array has wrong 4-byte ending unit” in application logs, and unexpected JVM crashes or new hs_err_pid log files. The exception is thrown after the overflow, so it indicates an attempt and not a blocked attack. Symantec and Carbon Black Security Response is investigating this vulnerability, guidance and reproduction steps. Full protection information is in the Symantec Protection Bulletin for Java4Shell . The bulletin will be updated continuously as new information becomes available. Symantec's Security Response organization develops and deploys new security content to Symantec customers. Our team of global threat analysts operate 24x7 to track developments on the threat landscape and protect Symantec customers.

sources.title: National Security Agency network for internal communications goes down | NSA - The Guardian
passages: The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down.

The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday.
Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage.
Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.”
“Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said.
“But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like.

A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong.

extraction.body: NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible. Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.” He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions. While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly. “Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like. “What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”

sources.title: US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline - BBC
passages: A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.
The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.

Last week, a massive Microsoft outage impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world - including the US and Canada - while a network failure grounded all US flights.

The NSA - America's largest intelligence organisation - said it had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" but that "mission-critical capabilities" were not affected. The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information. It comes after a string of technology outages in the US in recent days that have affected flights, banks and other infrastructure. "While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC. "NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events." It did not specify when the issue began, nor when it would be resolved. The issue was not a cyberattack, multiple US news outlets reported. Tens of thousands of people work at the NSA, which is responsible for collecting signals intelligence, overseeing cyber threats, and protecting US government communications. Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday. Sources familiar with the situation told CBS that operations at the NSA's headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, had not been affected but that some activities had been redirected to other facilities around the country. extraction.body: NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible. Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.” He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions. While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly. “Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like. “What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”

The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. coreStoryFacts.text: A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.
The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.

The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down.

The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday.
Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage.

The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information. It comes after a string of technology outages in the US in recent days that have affected flights, banks and other infrastructure. "While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC. extraction.body: NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible. Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.” He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions. While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly. “Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like. “What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”

The NSA episode is among a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions in the last week, including a system overload Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that caused ripple effects in the financial system and an internal systems outage at United Airlines that delayed departing flights. sources.title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off
passages: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.
The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training.
Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting.

Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users.
Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.
Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity.
For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled.
OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default.

extraction.body: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change , which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models. Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models. passages: 18 (local time), Taiwan media outlet IT Home reported that Google announced changes to Gemini's chat history and data use policies this week through an official blog and email.The key is separating chat history retention from consent for AI training.

After the policy change, chat data will be stored for about 2 months even if the history function is turned off.Google said the extended retention period is intended to strengthen safety and security in line with advances in AI systems.

Previously, the two functions were managed together through the Keep Activity setting, but going forward users can keep chat history while preventing their data from being used to train generative AI models.Google explained the move is aimed at strengthening users' control over personal information.

Whether the new retention period applies should be checked depending on the status of service updates.The overhaul widens users' options on AI training, but it is also expected to prolong discussion over privacy protection as conversation data remains on Google's servers for longer.
Previously, even if users disabled activity history, it kept conversations for up to 72 hours to provide the service and ensure safety.

passages: 18 (local time), Taiwan media outlet IT Home reported that Google announced changes to Gemini's chat history and data use policies this week through an official blog and email.The key is separating chat history retention from consent for AI training.

After the policy change, chat data will be stored for about 2 months even if the history function is turned off.Google said the extended retention period is intended to strengthen safety and security in line with advances in AI systems.

Previously, the two functions were managed together through the Keep Activity setting, but going forward users can keep chat history while preventing their data from being used to train generative AI models.Google explained the move is aimed at strengthening users' control over personal information.

Whether the new retention period applies should be checked depending on the status of service updates.The overhaul widens users' options on AI training, but it is also expected to prolong discussion over privacy protection as conversation data remains on Google's servers for longer.
Previously, even if users disabled activity history, it kept conversations for up to 72 hours to provide the service and ensure safety.

Google says this update is meant to boost safety and security.
And don't worry, Google confirms these stored chats won't be used to train its AI models.

extraction.body: Google's Gemini app is changing how it handles your chats: instead of deleting them after 72 hours, it'll now keep temporary chats for about two months, even if you turn chat history off. Google says this update is meant to boost safety and security. For context, OpenAI may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. Gemini now lets you control chat history and AI training separately, rather than bundling them together under "Keep Activity." If you've turned off Keep Activity before, both options will stay off by default. And don't worry, Google confirms these stored chats won't be used to train its AI models.

sources.title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
passages: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.
Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.
Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package.
OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents.
In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions.
These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files.
OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files.
It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package.
Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said.
How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said.
“Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis.
The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens.

extraction.body: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post. The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps. Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said. The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security. “This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said. OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. AI pipelines in focus OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access. It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. What security teams should do Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido. If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.

extraction.body: On November 17, 2026 at 20:35 UTC, versions 1.26.1 & 1.26.2 of the Microsoft PyPI package agent-framework were published with an added credential stealer. The package gets almost 200k downloads a month. The malicious versions have since been quarantined. At 20:35 UTC on November 17, 2026, a malicious version ( 1.26.1 ) of the agent-framework package (Microsoft Agent Framework) was uploaded to PyPI. A second version, 1.26.2 , followed at 21:08 UTC. As of 21:30 UTC, both versions were no longer available on PyPI. The package gets about 41,000 downloads a week. When a malicious version is installed, it drops a .pth file into the site-packages root ( agent_framework_meta.pth in 1.26.1, af_runtime_diag.pth in 1.26.2). Python runs .pth files on every interpreter start, so the credential stealer runs whenever Python starts in that environment, even if agent-framework is never imported. Updated Nov 18 14:00 UTC - Updated root cause and analyzed exfiltrated data. Wiz promptly reported these findings to Microsoft on the 17th. The attacker's tooling reported its own progress to the same publicly accessible webhook it used for exfiltration, which let Wiz Research observe part of the operation. The attacker appears to have compromised a client certificate and private key for Microsoft ESRP (Engineering System Release Pipeline), the internal service Microsoft uses to sign and publish this package. Their first publish attempt, from AWS, was rejected by ESRP's IP filtering. A second attempt from Microsoft-owned IP space succeeded. How the credentials were obtained is not yet known. The tooling identifies itself as Cairn , an open-source AI penetration-testing framework : it staged the package at /tmp/cairn_pkg and sent a CAIRN_ESRP_PROBE2 connectivity probe. Before publishing, the attacker ran the stealer on their own machine. That run captured an AI coding agent configuration that appears to be the open-source Pi harness backed by a GLM-family model ( pi_glm53 ), routed through a local proxy. Earlier this year, another Microsoft Python package, durabletask , was compromised after its PyPI token was stolen. We have not linked the two incidents. agent_framework_meta.pth contains one line: import agent_framework_meta In 1.26.1, agent_framework_meta/__init__.py then calls _telemetry._start() . The stealer forks into a detached session ( os.setsid()) , or falls back to a daemon thread where fork isn't available. It sets _AF_TEL=1 to avoid running again in child processes. The file and function names ( _telemetry , "Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook", user-agent af-runtime-diagnostics/1 ) are made to look like legitimate SDK telemetry. The stealer is focused on Azure and Azure DevOps. It collects: Environment variables with names containing strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, FOUNDRY, NPM, PIP, NUGET, SYSTEM, BUILD, AGENT Other processes' environments : secret-looking values read from up to 300 /proc/*/environ files .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json 1.26.2 was uploaded at 21:08 UTC, 33 minutes after 1.26.1. It is a repacked 1.26.1 that sends to the same webhook.site URL, with these changes: New trigger. agent_framework_meta/__init__.py is restored to the clean 1.26.0 file. Instead, a new top-level af_runtime_diag.pth imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py , which starts the stealer as soon as it is imported. Searching only for the 1.26.1 file names will miss this version. We have confirmed the attackers token was on the free tier, and a maximum of 50 requests were captured. However, those requests can contain working cloud, CI and registry credentials. Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intelligence Center advisory on this incident. Identify exposure: search lockfiles, CI logs, virtualenvs and container images for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. Pin to 1.26.0. Check for execution : look in site-packages for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py (1.26.1), or af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py (1.26.2). Any Python process started in that environment ran the payload. Check egress: search proxy and DNS logs for webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb . A 200 means that host's data was accepted. A 410/429 suggests it was rejected. Rotate credentials on affected hosts and runners: Azure CLI sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, npm/PyPI/NuGet/Docker/Hugging Face tokens, git credentials Audit Azure identities: review sign-in and activity logs for managed identities and federated credentials (workload identity federation) that were reachable from affected VMs, App Services, AKS nodes or ADO pipelines. Stolen managed-identity and OIDC-exchanged tokens are valid for up to 24 hours. For longer-term hardening guidance, see Practical Package Security: The Unofficial Guide . extraction.body: Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido , Chainguard , Endor Labs , OX Security , SafeDep , Socket , StepSecurity , and Google-owned Wiz . The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access. Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python. "Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report. Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported. "Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs said. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework." The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then launches the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data - "Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue new ones," SafeDep said. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those." "In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata." It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service ( IMDS ) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token. All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb"). Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables. Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps - "The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside." coreStoryFacts.text: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of agent-framework on PyPI steal Azure, Azure DevOps, and GitHub Actions credentials when Python starts.
Copyright © 2026 SecurityWeek ®, a Wired Business Media Publication.

Join to learn the four levels of architecting security into the agentic SDLC – from securing the code your developers' agents write to running a coordinated system of security agents you've built yourself.
Allie Mellen joined Microsoft as Principal Director, Security Research and Threat Intelligence.

Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.
Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.
Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package.
OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents.
In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions.
These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files.
OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files.
It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package.
Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said.
How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said.
“Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis.
The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens.
On November 17, 2026 at 20:35 UTC, versions 1.26.1 & 1.26.2 of the Microsoft PyPI package agent-framework were published with an added credential stealer.

The attacker appears to have compromised a client certificate and private key for Microsoft ESRP (Engineering System Release Pipeline), the internal service Microsoft uses to sign and publish this package.
Updated Nov 18 14:00 UTC - Updated root cause and analyzed exfiltrated data.
Wiz promptly reported these findings to Microsoft on the 17th.

Audit Azure identities: review sign-in and activity logs for managed identities and federated credentials (workload identity federation) that were reachable from affected VMs, App Services, AKS nodes or ADO pipelines.

Join to learn the four levels of architecting security into the agentic SDLC – from securing the code your developers' agents write to running a coordinated system of security agents you've built yourself.
Allie Mellen joined Microsoft as Principal Director, Security Research and Threat Intelligence.

Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.
Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.
Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package.
OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents.
In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions.
These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files.
OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files.
It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package.
Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said.
How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said.
“Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis.
The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens.
On November 17, 2026 at 20:35 UTC, versions 1.26.1 & 1.26.2 of the Microsoft PyPI package agent-framework were published with an added credential stealer.

The attacker appears to have compromised a client certificate and private key for Microsoft ESRP (Engineering System Release Pipeline), the internal service Microsoft uses to sign and publish this package.
Updated Nov 18 14:00 UTC - Updated root cause and analyzed exfiltrated data.
Wiz promptly reported these findings to Microsoft on the 17th.

Audit Azure identities: review sign-in and activity logs for managed identities and federated credentials (workload identity federation) that were reachable from affected VMs, App Services, AKS nodes or ADO pipelines.
agent_framework_meta.pth contains one line: import agent_framework_meta
The stealer is focused on Azure and Azure DevOps.
Environment variables with names containing strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, FOUNDRY, NPM, PIP, NUGET, SYSTEM, BUILD, AGENT
Earlier this year, another Microsoft Python package, durabletask , was compromised after its PyPI token was stolen.
Azure CLI sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, npm/PyPI/NuGet/Docker/Hugging Face tokens, git credentials
Meet the Wiz AI Security Agent, your newest security teammate to discover AI agents, understand their purpose, and expose hidden risks.
See how the Green Agent balanced security urgency with business continuity to turn a toxic combination into an executable remediation plan and ready-to-merge pull requests.
Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year.

In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm .
"The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said.
"While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside."
As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository.

"Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework."

"Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report.

extraction.body: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post. The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps. Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said. The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security. “This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said. OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. AI pipelines in focus OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access. It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. What security teams should do Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido. If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.

extraction.body: On November 17, 2026 at 20:35 UTC, versions 1.26.1 & 1.26.2 of the Microsoft PyPI package agent-framework were published with an added credential stealer. The package gets almost 200k downloads a month. The malicious versions have since been quarantined. At 20:35 UTC on November 17, 2026, a malicious version ( 1.26.1 ) of the agent-framework package (Microsoft Agent Framework) was uploaded to PyPI. A second version, 1.26.2 , followed at 21:08 UTC. As of 21:30 UTC, both versions were no longer available on PyPI. The package gets about 41,000 downloads a week. When a malicious version is installed, it drops a .pth file into the site-packages root ( agent_framework_meta.pth in 1.26.1, af_runtime_diag.pth in 1.26.2). Python runs .pth files on every interpreter start, so the credential stealer runs whenever Python starts in that environment, even if agent-framework is never imported. Updated Nov 18 14:00 UTC - Updated root cause and analyzed exfiltrated data. Wiz promptly reported these findings to Microsoft on the 17th. The attacker's tooling reported its own progress to the same publicly accessible webhook it used for exfiltration, which let Wiz Research observe part of the operation. The attacker appears to have compromised a client certificate and private key for Microsoft ESRP (Engineering System Release Pipeline), the internal service Microsoft uses to sign and publish this package. Their first publish attempt, from AWS, was rejected by ESRP's IP filtering. A second attempt from Microsoft-owned IP space succeeded. How the credentials were obtained is not yet known. The tooling identifies itself as Cairn , an open-source AI penetration-testing framework : it staged the package at /tmp/cairn_pkg and sent a CAIRN_ESRP_PROBE2 connectivity probe. Before publishing, the attacker ran the stealer on their own machine. That run captured an AI coding agent configuration that appears to be the open-source Pi harness backed by a GLM-family model ( pi_glm53 ), routed through a local proxy. Earlier this year, another Microsoft Python package, durabletask , was compromised after its PyPI token was stolen. We have not linked the two incidents. agent_framework_meta.pth contains one line: import agent_framework_meta In 1.26.1, agent_framework_meta/__init__.py then calls _telemetry._start() . The stealer forks into a detached session ( os.setsid()) , or falls back to a daemon thread where fork isn't available. It sets _AF_TEL=1 to avoid running again in child processes. The file and function names ( _telemetry , "Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook", user-agent af-runtime-diagnostics/1 ) are made to look like legitimate SDK telemetry. The stealer is focused on Azure and Azure DevOps. It collects: Environment variables with names containing strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, FOUNDRY, NPM, PIP, NUGET, SYSTEM, BUILD, AGENT Other processes' environments : secret-looking values read from up to 300 /proc/*/environ files .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json 1.26.2 was uploaded at 21:08 UTC, 33 minutes after 1.26.1. It is a repacked 1.26.1 that sends to the same webhook.site URL, with these changes: New trigger. agent_framework_meta/__init__.py is restored to the clean 1.26.0 file. Instead, a new top-level af_runtime_diag.pth imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py , which starts the stealer as soon as it is imported. Searching only for the 1.26.1 file names will miss this version. We have confirmed the attackers token was on the free tier, and a maximum of 50 requests were captured. However, those requests can contain working cloud, CI and registry credentials. Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intelligence Center advisory on this incident. Identify exposure: search lockfiles, CI logs, virtualenvs and container images for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. Pin to 1.26.0. Check for execution : look in site-packages for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py (1.26.1), or af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py (1.26.2). Any Python process started in that environment ran the payload. Check egress: search proxy and DNS logs for webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb . A 200 means that host's data was accepted. A 410/429 suggests it was rejected. Rotate credentials on affected hosts and runners: Azure CLI sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, npm/PyPI/NuGet/Docker/Hugging Face tokens, git credentials Audit Azure identities: review sign-in and activity logs for managed identities and federated credentials (workload identity federation) that were reachable from affected VMs, App Services, AKS nodes or ADO pipelines. Stolen managed-identity and OIDC-exchanged tokens are valid for up to 24 hours. For longer-term hardening guidance, see Practical Package Security: The Unofficial Guide .
