extraction.body: Nvidia has stopped shipping Hopper data centre chips to China despite receiving approval from the US government last year to sell a version of the processors to the country. The company sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper data centre products to China in the third quarter of fiscal 2027, Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim chief executive, said during the third-quarter FY 2027 earnings announcement on Tuesday. However, the company will not continue these shipments. "Our future guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre products to China," Kress said. The development marks a shift for Nvidia, which has spent years seeking greater access to the Chinese market. US President Donald Trump had approved the sale of H200 processors, part of Nvidia's Hopper generation, to China last year. The H200 chips are two generations behind the company's latest Rubin family of processors. Nvidia had also sought permission to sell its more advanced Blackwell chips to China, but the Trump administration did not approve the request. The Trump administration had, on Monday, moved to increase oversight of processor exports to several countries and restrict overseas chip sales where data centre operators could provide Chinese companies with remote access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and servers. Nvidia has also said that it was not assuming any data centre compute revenue from China in its outlook for the fourth quarter. Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter ended October 25, up 103 per cent year-on-year. Revenue from its data centre business rose 110 per cent to $107.6 billion. Net income more than doubled to $65.3 billion from $31.9 billion a year earlier. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent. The company also clarified that Nvidia's board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, following his departure from the company last week. Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said, "Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." The company is working with an executive search firm to identify a permanent successor, while considering both internal and external candidates. Kress, meanwhile, sought to reassure investors about the company's operations following the leadership change, describing the situation as business as usual.

passages: Nvidia Stops Sending Powerful AI Chips to China Despite US Approval Image Credits: AI

US-based chipmaker Nvidia has stopped shipping its powerful artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China, raising questions about the future of a special licensing arrangement between Washington and Beijing.

The development was confirmed by Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday. She said the company had no plans to make further shipments of licensed Hopper-generation data centre products to China.

Kress took over as interim CEO following Jensen Huang’s resignation last week. Her announcement has raised concerns about the future of Nvidia’s business in China, particularly as both countries continue to navigate restrictions on advanced semiconductor technology.
During the earnings call, Kress revealed that Nvidia had sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper-generation data centre products to China in the quarter that ended on October 25.
However, she made it clear that the company’s latest financial guidance does not include any further shipments of these products to the Chinese market.
“Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre products to China,” Kress said.
She did not provide a specific reason for the decision or clarify whether the suspension of shipments would be permanent.
Nvidia’s Hopper series includes some of the company’s powerful processors designed for artificial intelligence and data centre operations.
One of the key products in this range is the H200 chip, which is used to train and run advanced AI models.

These processors play an important role in handling the large amounts of computing power required for AI development. They are used by companies and research organisations to build and operate advanced AI systems.
Nvidia’s decision to stop shipments could therefore have implications for Chinese companies looking to access advanced computing hardware for their AI development.
The announcement has also raised questions about a special licensing arrangement negotiated between Washington and Beijing.
The agreement was expected to provide a way for Nvidia to sell certain advanced AI chips to Chinese customers under US licensing conditions.
However, with the company now confirming that it has stopped shipping licensed Hopper products to China, the future of these sales remains uncertain.
Nvidia has not explained whether the decision is linked to regulatory restrictions, business considerations or other factors.
For now, the company has indicated that further licensed Hopper-generation data centre shipments to China are not part of its current plans.

extraction.body: Nvidia has stopped shipping Hopper data centre chips to China despite receiving approval from the US government last year to sell a version of the processors to the country. The company sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper data centre products to China in the third quarter of fiscal 2027, Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim chief executive, said during the third-quarter FY 2027 earnings announcement on Tuesday. However, the company will not continue these shipments. "Our future guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre products to China," Kress said. The development marks a shift for Nvidia, which has spent years seeking greater access to the Chinese market. US President Donald Trump had approved the sale of H200 processors, part of Nvidia's Hopper generation, to China last year. The H200 chips are two generations behind the company's latest Rubin family of processors. Nvidia had also sought permission to sell its more advanced Blackwell chips to China, but the Trump administration did not approve the request. The Trump administration had, on Monday, moved to increase oversight of processor exports to several countries and restrict overseas chip sales where data centre operators could provide Chinese companies with remote access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and servers. Nvidia has also said that it was not assuming any data centre compute revenue from China in its outlook for the fourth quarter. Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter ended October 25, up 103 per cent year-on-year. Revenue from its data centre business rose 110 per cent to $107.6 billion. Net income more than doubled to $65.3 billion from $31.9 billion a year earlier. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent. The company also clarified that Nvidia's board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, following his departure from the company last week. Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said, "Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." The company is working with an executive search firm to identify a permanent successor, while considering both internal and external candidates. Kress, meanwhile, sought to reassure investors about the company's operations following the leadership change, describing the situation as business as usual.

extraction.body: A federal judge has ruled that outwitting trading bots on Ethereum is not wire fraud, throwing out the U.S. government’s first criminal case over a so-called MEV exploit that cleared two MIT-educated brothers whom prosecutors accused of making $25 million in 12 seconds. U.S. District Judge Jessica Clarke in Manhattan granted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno a judgment of acquittal on Nov. 16 on charges of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, according to her opinion . The ruling comes a year after a jury deadlocked and Clarke declared a mistrial in November 2025, and it directs the court clerk to close the case. “It is a trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use,” Clarke wrote of Ethereum. Pending Ethereum transactions sit in a public queue known as the mempool until a validator, the network participant chosen to add the next block, includes them. Trading bots monitor the queue to capture so-called maximal extractable value, or MEV, the profit available to whoever controls the sequence of transactions in a block. The most common bot play is the sandwich. A bot spots a large pending buy, buys the token just ahead of it, lets the victim’s purchase push the price up and sells straight into it. Most validators do not assemble their own blocks, and instead buy finished ones from specialized builders through onchain intermediaries known as relays. A relay keeps a block’s contents secret until the validator signs a promise to publish it, so the validator cannot peek at a builder’s trades and steal them. The brothers set a trap in April 2023, according to the court’s opinion. They placed eight bait transactions meant to attract sandwich bots — programs that buy just ahead of someone else’s trade and sell immediately after it — pocketing the price difference.

A US judge acquitted two MIT-educated brothers in a $25 million Ethereum fraud case. Judge Jessica Clarke ruled that prosecutors failed to establish material misrepresentation. Flashbots patched its relay software within 24 hours of the April 2023 MEV incident. Clarke ruled that prosecutors had failed to establish a material misrepresentation, an essential element of wire fraud. The decision clears the Massachusetts Institute of Technology-educated brothers of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Their trial ended in a mistrial in November 2025 after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict. US judge finds no material deception in Ethereum trading case Much of Clarke's ruling examined the rules governing Ethereum and whether participants make explicit or implicit promises when submitting transactions, registering validators or interacting with software used to organize blockchain transactions. “It is a trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use,” Clarke wrote, describing Ethereum. Federal prosecutors argued that the brothers' trading activity involved deception because they deliberately placed transactions designed to attract automated trading bots before disrupting the bots' intended trades. Clarke rejected the argument that submitting a transaction to Ethereum's public pool of pending transactions amounted to an agreement that it would be executed alongside other trades in a particular order. The judge found that the government's comparison with spoofing in traditional financial markets was equally problematic. Unlike orders placed with the intention of canceling them, the brothers' bait transactions were never withdrawn and appeared on the blockchain within approximately one minute of the operation. Neither Ethereum nor the MEV-Boost software specifications established the obligations that prosecutors claimed the brothers had violated, the ruling said. How the brothers made $25 million from Ethereum trading bots At the center of the prosecution was a trading operation called Omakase, which targeted cryptocurrency traders engaged in a practice known as sandwich trading. Court records show that the Peraire-Bueno brothers spent months preparing Omakase and registered 16 Ethereum validators capable of facilitating the operation. In April 2023, eight transactions attracted sandwich traders whose automated programs assembled trades intended to profit from the brothers' purchases. Using that information, the brothers altered the proposed arrangement of transactions, disrupting the sandwich traders' expected sales and generating approximately $25 million in profits. The brothers' validator incurred a penalty of 1 ETH for proposing two blocks during the same Ethereum block production slot. Court rejects prosecution's arguments over MEV-Boost software Another part of the government's case concerned invalid information contained in a digitally signed block header submitted to the Ultrasound Relay during Omakase. Clarke acknowledged that the information was incorrect, but trial evidence established that the relay did not examine the disputed fields before releasing the block's transaction data. The purportedly false information consequently “had no impact on the behavior of its recipient,” the judge wrote. Prosecutors did not present an expert witness on Ethereum's trading environment or call a representative from Ultrasound during the trial. Clarke cited the separate 2025 wire fraud ruling involving Mango Markets trader Avraham Eisenberg, where the court found that other users' expectations about the operation of a cryptocurrency platform did not establish that the defendant had made a false promise. Ethereum prosecution ends more than two years after arrests As crypto.news previously reported, U.S. authorities arrested the brothers in May 2024 following an investigation involving the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation unit. In July 2025, Clarke rejected an earlier motion to dismiss the fraud charges, although a separate charge of conspiracy to receive stolen property was dismissed after prosecutors decided not to pursue it. The November 2026 ruling found that the evidence presented at trial could not sustain the wire fraud charges. The money laundering conspiracy charge depended on the proceeds of the alleged fraud and therefore failed as well. Court records show that Flashbots temporarily blacklisted the validator involved in Omakase and updated its relay software within 24 hours of the incident. A cryptocurrency wallet containing $3 million of the proceeds was frozen, while the brothers had converted their remaining profits into U.S. dollars by October 2023.

extraction.body: A Manhattan federal judge has thrown out the criminal case against two MIT-educated brothers accused of draining about $25 million from Ethereum trading bots, ruling that prosecutors never proved the element of deception that wire fraud requires. U.S. District Judge Jessica Clarke granted a judgment of acquittal on Monday for Anton and James Peraire-Bueno, wiping away convictions on wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The ruling, which followed a defense motion, closes the case without a second trial after a jury deadlocked in November 2025. The decision turns on a narrow legal question rather than a verdict on the brothers' conduct. Clarke wrote that the court was not asked to decide whether the pair acted rightly or morally, or whether they broke laws that were never charged. What the government had to show was a material misrepresentation, and none of its theories established one, she found. Her reasoning leaned on the nature of the network itself. Ethereum, the judge noted, is a "trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use." While the brothers' scheme "may have frustrated the spirit" of MEV-Boost -- software that lets validators hand transaction ordering to specialized block builders -- that was not enough to turn the conduct into fraud, she said. In a footnote, Clarke added that the prosecution "raises serious due process concerns," though she declined to rule on that point. The money laundering count fell along with the fraud charges because it depended on the same alleged proceeds. The case dates to April 2023, when, according to the ruling, the brothers planted bait transactions meant to draw in specific sandwich bots -- automated traders that profit from maximal extractable value by placing trades on both sides of other users' orders. They then exploited a flaw in a relay's code to see the bots' bundled trades before committing a block, swapped the bait for trades that sold the tokens instead, and left the bots with roughly $25 million in losses in about 12 seconds. Federal agents arrested the pair in May 2024, alleging months of planning and steps to conceal the proceeds. At the first trial, an insider testified that the brothers had planned the attack, and the defense had earlier tried to keep evidence of their Google searches out of court. Jurors could not agree on a verdict, prompting the mistrial. Clarke's ruling described the matter as a "first of its kind" prosecution, a phrase the government itself used in its indictment. The ruling also cited a 2025 decision in the case of Mango Markets trader Avraham Eisenberg, where a judge found insufficient evidence of false representations. Crypto policy advocates framed the outcome as a check on prosecutorial reach. Coin Center executive director Peter Van Valkenburgh called the acquittal "excellent news," warning that the government's honest-validator theory could have let prosecutors impose their own standards of conduct on Ethereum validators through wire fraud law. "Anyone participating in an open network would have to wonder whether prosecutors might later declare their behavior 'dishonest' and haul them into court," he said. Those are his views, not language from the ruling. The acquittal resolves the charged case, not every question the allegations raised. It does not decide whether the conduct was ethical or whether other statutes might reach it, and it sets no blanket rule for MEV strategies generally. The outcome rested on this indictment's evidence and legal theory, and the available record identifies no new regulation or legislative action prompted by the decision. Market data offered little sign that traders repriced Ether on the news. At 12:13 UTC on Tuesday, CoinGecko showed ETH at $1,811.16, up 1.05% over 24 hours, while Bitcoin traded at $64,784, up 1.32%. Both assets remained deeply lower over the prior week, and the Crypto Fear & Greed Index sat at 12, in "Extreme Fear" territory, according to Alternative.me. Note: Prices and changes from CoinGecko data cited in market coverage; a single session's move does not establish that the ruling drove trading. For investors, the supported reading is narrow: a federal judge found the government failed to prove a required element of wire fraud and ended the prosecution. The ruling leaves open how future cases treat conduct on public networks and whether lawmakers or regulators will draw clearer boundaries around transaction-ordering practices. extraction.body: A federal judge has ruled that outwitting trading bots on Ethereum is not wire fraud, throwing out the U.S. government’s first criminal case over a so-called MEV exploit that cleared two MIT-educated brothers whom prosecutors accused of making $25 million in 12 seconds. U.S. District Judge Jessica Clarke in Manhattan granted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno a judgment of acquittal on Nov. 16 on charges of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, according to her opinion . The ruling comes a year after a jury deadlocked and Clarke declared a mistrial in November 2025, and it directs the court clerk to close the case. “It is a trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use,” Clarke wrote of Ethereum. Pending Ethereum transactions sit in a public queue known as the mempool until a validator, the network participant chosen to add the next block, includes them. Trading bots monitor the queue to capture so-called maximal extractable value, or MEV, the profit available to whoever controls the sequence of transactions in a block. The most common bot play is the sandwich. A bot spots a large pending buy, buys the token just ahead of it, lets the victim’s purchase push the price up and sells straight into it. Most validators do not assemble their own blocks, and instead buy finished ones from specialized builders through onchain intermediaries known as relays. A relay keeps a block’s contents secret until the validator signs a promise to publish it, so the validator cannot peek at a builder’s trades and steal them. The brothers set a trap in April 2023, according to the court’s opinion. They placed eight bait transactions meant to attract sandwich bots — programs that buy just ahead of someone else’s trade and sell immediately after it — pocketing the price difference.

extraction.body: A U.S. federal judge has acquitted brothers Anton and James Peraire-Bueno of criminal charges stemming from a $25 million Ethereum trading operation that prosecutors alleged was executed in just 12 seconds. A US judge acquitted two MIT-educated brothers in a $25 million Ethereum fraud case. Judge Jessica Clarke ruled that prosecutors failed to establish material misrepresentation. The Ethereum MEV operation generated $25 million in profits within just 12 seconds. The acquittal follows a November 2025 mistrial after jurors failed to reach a verdict. Flashbots patched its relay software within 24 hours of the April 2023 MEV incident. Clarke ruled that prosecutors had failed to establish a material misrepresentation, an essential element of wire fraud. The decision clears the Massachusetts Institute of Technology-educated brothers of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Their trial ended in a mistrial in November 2025 after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict. US judge finds no material deception in Ethereum trading case Much of Clarke's ruling examined the rules governing Ethereum and whether participants make explicit or implicit promises when submitting transactions, registering validators or interacting with software used to organize blockchain transactions. “It is a trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use,” Clarke wrote, describing Ethereum. Federal prosecutors argued that the brothers' trading activity involved deception because they deliberately placed transactions designed to attract automated trading bots before disrupting the bots' intended trades. Clarke rejected the argument that submitting a transaction to Ethereum's public pool of pending transactions amounted to an agreement that it would be executed alongside other trades in a particular order. The judge found that the government's comparison with spoofing in traditional financial markets was equally problematic. Unlike orders placed with the intention of canceling them, the brothers' bait transactions were never withdrawn and appeared on the blockchain within approximately one minute of the operation. Neither Ethereum nor the MEV-Boost software specifications established the obligations that prosecutors claimed the brothers had violated, the ruling said. How the brothers made $25 million from Ethereum trading bots At the center of the prosecution was a trading operation called Omakase, which targeted cryptocurrency traders engaged in a practice known as sandwich trading. Court records show that the Peraire-Bueno brothers spent months preparing Omakase and registered 16 Ethereum validators capable of facilitating the operation. In April 2023, eight transactions attracted sandwich traders whose automated programs assembled trades intended to profit from the brothers' purchases. Using that information, the brothers altered the proposed arrangement of transactions, disrupting the sandwich traders' expected sales and generating approximately $25 million in profits. The brothers' validator incurred a penalty of 1 ETH for proposing two blocks during the same Ethereum block production slot. Court rejects prosecution's arguments over MEV-Boost software Another part of the government's case concerned invalid information contained in a digitally signed block header submitted to the Ultrasound Relay during Omakase. Clarke acknowledged that the information was incorrect, but trial evidence established that the relay did not examine the disputed fields before releasing the block's transaction data. The purportedly false information consequently “had no impact on the behavior of its recipient,” the judge wrote. Prosecutors did not present an expert witness on Ethereum's trading environment or call a representative from Ultrasound during the trial. Clarke cited the separate 2025 wire fraud ruling involving Mango Markets trader Avraham Eisenberg, where the court found that other users' expectations about the operation of a cryptocurrency platform did not establish that the defendant had made a false promise. Ethereum prosecution ends more than two years after arrests As crypto.news previously reported, U.S. authorities arrested the brothers in May 2024 following an investigation involving the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation unit. In July 2025, Clarke rejected an earlier motion to dismiss the fraud charges, although a separate charge of conspiracy to receive stolen property was dismissed after prosecutors decided not to pursue it. The November 2026 ruling found that the evidence presented at trial could not sustain the wire fraud charges. The money laundering conspiracy charge depended on the proceeds of the alleged fraud and therefore failed as well. Court records show that Flashbots temporarily blacklisted the validator involved in Omakase and updated its relay software within 24 hours of the incident. A cryptocurrency wallet containing $3 million of the proceeds was frozen, while the brothers had converted their remaining profits into U.S. dollars by October 2023.

extraction.body: A Manhattan federal judge has thrown out the criminal case against two MIT-educated brothers accused of draining about $25 million from Ethereum trading bots, ruling that prosecutors never proved the element of deception that wire fraud requires. U.S. District Judge Jessica Clarke granted a judgment of acquittal on Monday for Anton and James Peraire-Bueno, wiping away convictions on wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The ruling, which followed a defense motion, closes the case without a second trial after a jury deadlocked in November 2025. The decision turns on a narrow legal question rather than a verdict on the brothers' conduct. Clarke wrote that the court was not asked to decide whether the pair acted rightly or morally, or whether they broke laws that were never charged. What the government had to show was a material misrepresentation, and none of its theories established one, she found. Her reasoning leaned on the nature of the network itself. Ethereum, the judge noted, is a "trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use." While the brothers' scheme "may have frustrated the spirit" of MEV-Boost -- software that lets validators hand transaction ordering to specialized block builders -- that was not enough to turn the conduct into fraud, she said. In a footnote, Clarke added that the prosecution "raises serious due process concerns," though she declined to rule on that point. The money laundering count fell along with the fraud charges because it depended on the same alleged proceeds. The case dates to April 2023, when, according to the ruling, the brothers planted bait transactions meant to draw in specific sandwich bots -- automated traders that profit from maximal extractable value by placing trades on both sides of other users' orders. They then exploited a flaw in a relay's code to see the bots' bundled trades before committing a block, swapped the bait for trades that sold the tokens instead, and left the bots with roughly $25 million in losses in about 12 seconds. Federal agents arrested the pair in May 2024, alleging months of planning and steps to conceal the proceeds. At the first trial, an insider testified that the brothers had planned the attack, and the defense had earlier tried to keep evidence of their Google searches out of court. Jurors could not agree on a verdict, prompting the mistrial. Clarke's ruling described the matter as a "first of its kind" prosecution, a phrase the government itself used in its indictment. The ruling also cited a 2025 decision in the case of Mango Markets trader Avraham Eisenberg, where a judge found insufficient evidence of false representations. Crypto policy advocates framed the outcome as a check on prosecutorial reach. Coin Center executive director Peter Van Valkenburgh called the acquittal "excellent news," warning that the government's honest-validator theory could have let prosecutors impose their own standards of conduct on Ethereum validators through wire fraud law. "Anyone participating in an open network would have to wonder whether prosecutors might later declare their behavior 'dishonest' and haul them into court," he said. Those are his views, not language from the ruling. The acquittal resolves the charged case, not every question the allegations raised. It does not decide whether the conduct was ethical or whether other statutes might reach it, and it sets no blanket rule for MEV strategies generally. The outcome rested on this indictment's evidence and legal theory, and the available record identifies no new regulation or legislative action prompted by the decision. Market data offered little sign that traders repriced Ether on the news. At 12:13 UTC on Tuesday, CoinGecko showed ETH at $1,811.16, up 1.05% over 24 hours, while Bitcoin traded at $64,784, up 1.32%. Both assets remained deeply lower over the prior week, and the Crypto Fear & Greed Index sat at 12, in "Extreme Fear" territory, according to Alternative.me. Note: Prices and changes from CoinGecko data cited in market coverage; a single session's move does not establish that the ruling drove trading. For investors, the supported reading is narrow: a federal judge found the government failed to prove a required element of wire fraud and ended the prosecution. The ruling leaves open how future cases treat conduct on public networks and whether lawmakers or regulators will draw clearer boundaries around transaction-ordering practices. SINGAPORE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency ⁠exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets next year and has no need to raise funds as its finances are sound, its ⁠regional business head told Reuters, even after arecord $6.3 billion was stolen in a hack last month. "We have ongoing conversations with at least five ‌or six markets ... three of which are in quite mature stages," SB Seker, Binance's APAC head, told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. "The others are ongoing conversations." He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in 15 markets, was looking at, but said South and Southeast Asia were key priorities and that details of the planned expansion ​were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of next year. Binance's expansion plans come ⁠on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea ⁠that resulted in $6.3 billion being stolen from its platform last month. The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, ⁠but ‌Pyongyang has denied that. The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier this month after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week. Binance used company money to buy replacement tokens and worked with industry partners to ⁠freeze $3 billion worth of the stolen assets. The exchange said in asocial media post last week ​that it had completed coverage of assets impacted ‌in the hack. Asked about the impact of those purchases on its balance sheet, Seker said the amount was "statistically ... not a large ⁠amount," adding that Binance would ​not need to raise fresh funds to absorb the costs. "I'm not downplaying the incident. I'm just saying as a metric," he said. "In terms of the impact to us, we can take the impact and we can weather it without any change to the way we operate." Seker said the company publishes its "proof-of-reserves," which show what crypto tokens it holds for customers, though it ⁠does not share its financial statements - including profit and loss statements, balance sheets and ​cash flow figures - with investors, including Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX. "We focus our public information on the verifiability of actual customer assets," he said. "But P&L, we do not publish ... we don't publish that to anyone, across the board. And that's entirely consistent with the private company setup." The Binance heist, which was the largest known crypto theft, hasrenewed ⁠scrutiny of cyber risks in the crypto industry. Seker said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded. "Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present," he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations. Binance said the Abu Dhabi Global Market's ​Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator and it pays taxes in jurisdictions where it has a taxable ⁠presence, as required by local laws. The firm does not have a formally established headquarters. Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond ​the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry. "The conversations now are 'well, this is ‌an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?' ​It's moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation," he said. "We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore." SINGAPORE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency ⁠exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets next year and has no need to raise funds as its finances are sound, its ⁠regional business head told Reuters, even after arecord $6.3 billion was stolen in a hack last month. "We have ongoing conversations with at least five ‌or six markets ... three of which are in quite mature stages," SB Seker, Binance's APAC head, told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. "The others are ongoing conversations." He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in 15 markets, was looking at, but said South and Southeast Asia were key priorities and that details of the planned expansion ​were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of next year. Binance's expansion plans come ⁠on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea ⁠that resulted in $6.3 billion being stolen from its platform last month. The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, ⁠but ‌Pyongyang has denied that. The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier this month after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week. Binance used company money to buy replacement tokens and worked with industry partners to ⁠freeze $3 billion worth of the stolen assets. The exchange said in asocial media post last week ​that it had completed coverage of assets impacted ‌in the hack. Asked about the impact of those purchases on its balance sheet, Seker said the amount was "statistically ... not a large ⁠amount," adding that Binance would ​not need to raise fresh funds to absorb the costs. "I'm not downplaying the incident. I'm just saying as a metric," he said. "In terms of the impact to us, we can take the impact and we can weather it without any change to the way we operate." Seker said the company publishes its "proof-of-reserves," which show what crypto tokens it holds for customers, though it ⁠does not share its financial statements - including profit and loss statements, balance sheets and ​cash flow figures - with investors, including Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX. "We focus our public information on the verifiability of actual customer assets," he said. "But P&L, we do not publish ... we don't publish that to anyone, across the board. And that's entirely consistent with the private company setup." The Binance heist, which was the largest known crypto theft, hasrenewed ⁠scrutiny of cyber risks in the crypto industry. Seker said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded. "Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present," he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations. Binance said the Abu Dhabi Global Market's ​Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator and it pays taxes in jurisdictions where it has a taxable ⁠presence, as required by local laws. The firm does not have a formally established headquarters. Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond ​the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry. "The conversations now are 'well, this is ‌an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?' ​It's moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation," he said. "We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore." "We have ongoing conversations with at least five ‌or six markets ... three of which are in quite mature stages," SB Seker, Binance's APAC head, told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. "The others are ongoing conversations."

He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in 15 markets, was looking at, but said South and Southeast Asia were key priorities and that details of the planned expansion ​were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of next year.
Binance's expansion plans come ⁠on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea ⁠that resulted in $6.3 billion being stolen from its platform last month.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, ⁠but ‌Pyongyang has denied that.

The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier this month after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week.

Binance used company money to buy replacement tokens and worked with industry partners to ⁠freeze $3 billion worth of the stolen assets. The exchange said in asocial media post last week ​that it had completed coverage of assets impacted ‌in the hack.

Asked about the impact of those purchases on its balance sheet, Seker said the amount was "statistically ... not a large ⁠amount," adding that Binance would ​not need to raise fresh funds to absorb the costs.
"I'm not downplaying the incident. I'm just saying as a metric," he said. "In terms of the impact to us, we can take the impact and we can weather it without any change to the way we operate."

Seker said the company publishes its "proof-of-reserves," which show what crypto tokens it holds for customers, though it ⁠does not share its financial statements - including profit and loss statements, balance sheets and ​cash flow figures - with investors, including Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX.

"We focus our public information on the verifiability of actual customer assets," he said. "But P&L, we do not publish ... we don't publish that to anyone, across the board. And that's entirely consistent with the private company setup."
The Binance heist, which was the largest known crypto theft, hasrenewed ⁠scrutiny of cyber risks in the crypto industry.

Seker said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded.
"Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present," he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations.

Binance said the Abu Dhabi Global Market's ​Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator and it pays taxes in jurisdictions where it has a taxable ⁠presence, as required by local laws. The firm does not have a formally established headquarters.
Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond ​the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry.

"The conversations now are 'well, this is ‌an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?' ​It's moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation," he said.

REUTERS/Manuel Orbegozo Richard Teng, Co-CEO at Binance, takes part in a talk during the Semafor "Silicon Valley & The World" Conference in San Francisco, California, US, November 16, 2026. REUTERS/Manuel Orbegozo SINGAPORE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets next year and has no need to raise funds as its finances are sound, its regional business head told Reuters, even after a record $6.3 billion was stolen in a hack last month. "We have ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets ... three of which are in quite mature stages," SB Seker, Binance's APAC head, told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. "The others are ongoing conversations." He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in 15 markets, was looking at, but said South and Southeast Asia were key priorities and that details of the planned expansion were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of next year. Binance's expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in $6.3 billion being stolen from its platform last month. The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier this month after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week. Binance used company money to buy replacement tokens and worked with industry partners to freeze $3 billion worth of the stolen assets. The exchange said in a social media post last week that it had completed coverage of assets impacted in the hack. Asked about the impact of those purchases on its balance sheet, Seker said the amount was "statistically ... not a large amount," adding that Binance would not need to raise fresh funds to absorb the costs. "I'm not downplaying the incident. I'm just saying as a metric," he said. "In terms of the impact to us, we can take the impact and we can weather it without any change to the way we operate." Seker said the company publishes its "proof-of-reserves," which show what crypto tokens it holds for customers, though it does not share its financial statements - including profit and loss statements, balance sheets and cash flow figures - with investors, including Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX. "We focus our public information on the verifiability of actual customer assets," he said. "But P&L, we do not publish ... we don't publish that to anyone, across the board. And that's entirely consistent with the private company setup." The Binance heist, which was the largest known crypto theft, has renewed scrutiny of cyber risks in the crypto industry. Seker said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded. "Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present," he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations. Binance said the Abu Dhabi Global Market's Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator and it pays taxes in jurisdictions where it has a taxable presence, as required by local laws. The firm does not have a formally established headquarters. Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry. "The conversations now are 'well, this is an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?' It's moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation," he said. "We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore."

extraction.body: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI , a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. But it’s the scenes between the over-the-top and somewhat repetitive action scenes that really make this Grand Theft Auto stand out. Almost every explosive gunfight or high-speed car chase is counterpointed by a sublimely dull, lightly interactive moment of mere routine existence: grilling burgers with pals by the water, playing fetch with a random dog, helping a neighbor tune up a car, or joking around over 18 holes of mini golf. Taken together, the juxtaposition lends a sense of surreal hyperreality to the goings-on in Vice City and its environs. Each of the game’s two sides gives the other a chance to breathe, forming a series of emotional peaks and valleys that stretch across a truly gargantuan amount of detailed simulation and pure gaming content. Grand Theft Auto VI never lets you get too settled with a budding life of crime or a budding family life. And it’s all the better for it. A large part of why this works so well is Jason and Lucia, the dual protagonists whose relationship drives the story. While that relationship starts off a bit awkwardly—thanks chiefly to Lucia’s brief prison stint—it quickly develops into a true criminal and life partnership. Both sides of the relationship are driven by a mutual desire to move up in the criminal world and eventually settle down to a legit family life, if they can just earn enough from the next big score. Of the two, Jason is definitely the duller partner. An ex-military meathead with a ripped body and a dull, affect-free vocal delivery, a decent chunk of Jason’s lines essentially boil down to “Yeah, sure, that’s fine.” While the game struggles to expose a bit of a tender and thoughtful side hiding underneath Jason’s cool demeanor, the writing can’t quite break through the emotionless masculine facade that Jason wears as a semi-permanent mask. Lucia is much more interesting as a vivacious and amiable Latina eager to grab any opportunity presented to her. The game takes some time to dig into the difficulties of Lucia’s underprivileged youth and highlight her strained relationship with an unreliable mother, helping to add some important depth to her chip-on-her-shoulder journey of self-improvement. And even the boring Jason seems that much more appealing seen through the lens of Lucia’s good-natured teasing and genuine affection. While Jason and Lucia can and do operate independently—and the game lets you change between them frequently—it’s their moments of togetherness that really stand out. There’s an easy, rom-com comfort to their time together, whether they’re discussing their future on the couch (“I feel like I haven’t done anything normal in a minute”), taking some time for quick romance (the game cuts away before things get too hot and heavy), or laying down covering fire for each other during a firefight (the lack of a co-op mode for these missions feels truly baffling). There’s a minor relationship simulation component to the game, with a simple “heart level” that can rise or fall based on some basic decisions. Don’t expect a lot of dating-sim style drama, though; as long as you make the completely obvious choices when they’re presented, it’s hard to let the relationship fall apart. That’s a good thing, too, because this is a relationship that’s easy to root for, even when the participants are literally getting away with murder. In true Grand Theft Auto fashion, Jason and Lucia’s particular way of chasing The American Dream is through a life of crime. Their travels through the criminal underworld start off kind of slow, as Lucia’s begging gradually compels Jason to reluctantly introduce her to the two-bit operators with which he’s found himself involved. For the first half of the game, the pair are constantly interacting with a rogues’ gallery of new criminal acquaintances, each more over-the-top than the last, and all of them having specific needs that somehow only Jason and Lucia can fulfill. Many of the missions these small-time crooks have on offer end up feeling like the criminal equivalent of errands—drive here, take that, lose the cops, repeat. It isn’t until the back half of the game that the main storyline really starts to focus on what it does best: integrating Jason and Lucia into a persistent ring of professional criminals working toward bigger and bigger scores. Here, the missions build on each other, with characters going undercover, casing targets, and learning new skills that eventually come together in some truly tense and bombastic heists. These missions also do the best job of showing off the dual protagonist system, frequently shifting the perspective between Jason and Lucia to highlight their different skills and views on how things are going down. Outside of this core plot, though, many of the missions and side stories in GTA VI make Jason and Lucia feel like side characters in their own story. I found myself beginning to tune out during some of the many missions in which one or both protagonists serve as glorified security props or overpaid getaway drivers amid other characters’ contrived turf wars. And even dozens of hours into the game, there were still missions that felt like tutorials, seemingly built around the opportunity to introduce some new simulation system or control scheme. Through it all, the game can’t seem to totally shake the style of sophomoric humor that feels a lot less “edgy” today than it did when Grand Theft Auto III hit back in 2001 (for players who are old enough to remember that release , at least). There are countless extended bits where the entire joke seems to boil down to “Man, kinky sex is weird, isn’t it?” or “Hey look, it’s a male penis (or something that looks similar to one).” And the game seems to take particular pleasure in forcing Jason into uncomfortable situations with plenty of T&A, much to Lucia’s good-natured bemusement. A word of warning for parents: This is a game that definitely earns a hard “M for Mature” rating and shows how standards for that rating have shifted since GTA: San Andreas earned an AO re-rating for hiding a single sex scene amid its legacy code. There are moments where GTA VI ’s satire cuts a bit deeper. I especially liked a couple of side stories that skewered buzzword-spewing crypto bros and multi-level marketing schemes with some welcome over-the-top excess. Overall, though, the game’s warmed-over one-liner takes on “wokeness” felt about as fresh as jokes about mothers-in-law and TV dinners, without much in the way of thought-provoking statements on society as a whole in 2026. Grand Theft Auto VI has a gift for finding excuses to lure you into an expertly designed space and then throwing together a reason for why you have to shoot/punch your way out. That might sound snarky, but I actually mean it more or less sincerely; I was frequently surprised by the scenarios the writers dreamed up to turn what seemed like a routine trip to some beautiful locale into a firefight with way more armed goons than seems strictly necessary. The moment-to-moment shooting will feel very familiar to Grand Theft Auto fans, by which I mean it’s dead simple to hide behind convenient cover and pop up to pick off relatively stupid enemies one by one with a dizzying array of available weaponry. The rare enemies that do manage to flank you seem to have incredibly bad aim, even at close range, and both Jason and Lucia can take a whole lot more punishment than the average quick-to-crumble grunt. Driving around town is significantly more exciting—you’ll be darting between cars in heavy traffic to chase down antagonists, avoid the police, or simply get where you’re going faster. It’s still a blast to sample as many vehicles as you can, from zippy but easy-to-wreck sports cars to tank-like trucks that can plow through traffic, tiny motorbikes that can squeeze through tight spaces, and off-road vehicles that can explore off the beaten path. Driving through the city also offers ample opportunities to get distracted from your main goals by dozens of side activities that dot the map. Even as I struggled to work through the story on deadline, I found myself getting sucked in for hours trying to master drone racing, chasing gold medals in countless mud-splattered rally races, or hunting for one of the many meditation spots hidden in out-of-the-way corners. While most of these side activities offer money or improve character stats, some are simply there to be experienced. Completionists will have a bear of a time tracking down every single hidden collectible, rare car, robbable location, and beautiful landmark the developers have placed throughout the city. Grand Theft Auto VI seems set to be one of those games you can just load up to hang out in long after the main story missions are done. Even with a fast vehicle, much of that “hang out” time can be spent simply crossing the game’s massive map. Getting from the depths of the wilderness in the north to the tip of the keys in the south is a six-plus-mile trip (measured at an apparently real-world-accurate scale) that can take 10 minutes to weave your way across on a good traffic day. During these cross-city treks, the tenor of the city’s architecture morphs noticeably as you pass from rich gated communities through the glitzy skyscraper-laden downtown and on to downtrodden neighborhoods, backwoods swamps, and laid-back island beach communities. As nice as Vice City’s outdoor architecture is, GTA VI’ s interiors are where the game’s developers really show off. Practically every story mission seems to introduce a new cavernous indoor space that’s fully furnished and lovingly crafted to look naturally lived-in and also utterly unlike anything you’ve seen before. And while you can’t go into every one of the thousands of buildings you pass on the streets of Vice City, you can enter a surprisingly large number, each with its own distinct layout and decorations. Another element that makes all these spaces feel lived-in is the game’s surprisingly detailed crowd system. Grand Theft Auto VI sometimes packs over a hundred non-player characters into a single space, with no two characters looking or acting alike in size, shape, dress, or animation. Working your way through these crowds can be integral to some of the game’s missions, but even when you’re just casually exploring, it’s fun to take advantage of eavesdropping opportunities, listening in on individual conversations that build into overlapping chatter (realistically muffled through walls and over distance). Grand Theft Auto VI ’s spaces also seem specifically designed to show off the game’s incredible lighting system, which really shines on a PS5 Pro. The effect is most apparent at night, when car headlights streaming through a window or the rotating blue-and-red of a cop car can cast the entire world in an otherworldly glow. But even in “normal” lighting conditions, I’d occasionally find myself slack-jawed at the details: a laptop screen partially reflected in a character’s glasses, the way rotating pyrotechnic laser effects played across dancers in a crowded club, the fluttering shadows cast by a leafy tree near sunset, or the finger smudges visible on your cell phone in bright sunshine. I could go on and on about the little “attention to detail” touches that add up to a more engaging world simulation. Characters who fall in the dirt get dust on only the specific parts of their clothes that hit the ground. Older characters look distinctly wrinkly, with veins that show through their thinning skin. Fabric and hair flow naturally in the wind and as characters move. Rain beads on car roofs and drips off overhangs during a storm. Through it all, one moment really stood out to me. As I prepared for an upcoming firefight, I had Lucia start eating some chips to buff her health. Halfway through the bag, I had her pick up a nearby soda, too. At first, Lucia held the chip bag in one hand and used the other to pick out individual chips. But once that other hand was occupied with a soda, she started shaking the bag above her head to pour the chips directly into her mouth. When I thought about the effort that went into coding and recording that specific animation for such a highly specific edge case, I thought about the millions of man-hours that went into making Grand Theft Auto VI the ultimate expression of this kind of urban crime/life sim. It might be a long time before we see this level of focused effort on a singular interactive vision again. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

Grand Theft Auto VI begins worldwide release after a 13-year wait, with players able to start playing as local clocks strike midnight on November 19. Connor Cattermoul, a 27-year-old New Zealander, said after completing GTA 6's introductory mission that it is "amazing" so far and that it "feels really smooth - there's so many little things you can do." Jason Waller, 56, from Bedford, said he has booked two days of annual leave and told BBC News that "I love the freedom of GTA," adding "You can leave the missions and wander off and discover so much." Rockstar Games' release schedule described in multiple guides sets a staggered rollout, with New Zealand reaching midnight Nov. 19 first and the UK waiting until midnight GMT on 19 November. The BBC also reported that gaming livestreamer Alana Black, known as Alana CJ on Twitch, said she will spend the day avoiding spoilers and warned, "You can be banned for it," about the "New Zealand trick." Game Informer said Leonida is "a joy to explore" and described the game as making "many ordinary tasks as compelling as the illegal ones." GTA 6 launches globally after a 13-year wait, with staggered rollout starting in New Zealand. Early reviews praise graphics and world design, and highlight smooth gameplay and strong narrative.
Grand Theft Auto VI begins worldwide release after a 13-year wait, with players able to start playing as local clocks strike midnight on November 19.

Connor Cattermoul, a 27-year-old New Zealander, said after completing GTA 6's introductory mission that it is "amazing" so far and that it "feels really smooth - there's so many little things you can do."

Jason Waller, 56, from Bedford, said he has booked two days of annual leave and told BBC News that "I love the freedom of GTA," adding "You can leave the missions and wander off and discover so much."
Rockstar Games' release schedule described in multiple guides sets a staggered rollout, with New Zealand reaching midnight Nov. 19 first and the UK waiting until midnight GMT on 19 November.

The BBC also reported that gaming livestreamer Alana Black, known as Alana CJ on Twitch, said she will spend the day avoiding spoilers and warned, "You can be banned for it," about the "New Zealand trick."

Ars Technica framed GTA VI as a contrast between action and everyday life, describing "the mundanities of everyday life" alongside "action movie bombast." The Ars Technica review also highlighted how "Almost every explosive gunfight or high-speed car chase" is counterpointed by "a sublimely dull, lightly interactive moment of mere routine existence." IGN said that after almost 120 hours it had "zero plans to stop playing it," and it described Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as "an interesting pair of playable characters."

Game Informer said Leonida is "a joy to explore" and described the game as making "many ordinary tasks as compelling as the illegal ones." COGconnected said the world spans "5 regions" and described the map as "a huge map with different biomes," including "the southern areas" and "the northern regions."

Rockstar Games is using local release times, and one guide says the game will become playable at midnight local time across all regions, making the exact unlock depend on a player's digital storefront settings.

The same Clarin guide described the Xbox workaround as the "New Zealand trick," and it said PS5 users can do it "but it requires purchasing the game through a separate account tied to that specific region."

Clarin also said GTA 6 pre-loading is available and warned that the game requires "up to 212 GB of free SSD space," so players who wait for launch time could be stuck watching a progress bar instead of playing.

coreStoryFacts.text: This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI , a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple.

That might sound snarky, but I actually mean it more or less sincerely; I was frequently surprised by the scenarios the writers dreamed up to turn what seemed like a routine trip to some beautiful locale into a firefight with way more armed goons than seems strictly necessary.
While most of these side activities offer money or improve character stats, some are simply there to be experienced.
Completionists will have a bear of a time tracking down every single hidden collectible, rare car, robbable location, and beautiful landmark the developers have placed throughout the city.
Another element that makes all these spaces feel lived-in is the game’s surprisingly detailed crowd system.
The effect is most apparent at night, when car headlights streaming through a window or the rotating blue-and-red of a cop car can cast the entire world in an otherworldly glow.
It might be a long time before we see this level of focused effort on a singular interactive vision again.

extraction.body: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI , a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. But it’s the scenes between the over-the-top and somewhat repetitive action scenes that really make this Grand Theft Auto stand out. Almost every explosive gunfight or high-speed car chase is counterpointed by a sublimely dull, lightly interactive moment of mere routine existence: grilling burgers with pals by the water, playing fetch with a random dog, helping a neighbor tune up a car, or joking around over 18 holes of mini golf. Taken together, the juxtaposition lends a sense of surreal hyperreality to the goings-on in Vice City and its environs. Each of the game’s two sides gives the other a chance to breathe, forming a series of emotional peaks and valleys that stretch across a truly gargantuan amount of detailed simulation and pure gaming content. Grand Theft Auto VI never lets you get too settled with a budding life of crime or a budding family life. And it’s all the better for it. A large part of why this works so well is Jason and Lucia, the dual protagonists whose relationship drives the story. While that relationship starts off a bit awkwardly—thanks chiefly to Lucia’s brief prison stint—it quickly develops into a true criminal and life partnership. Both sides of the relationship are driven by a mutual desire to move up in the criminal world and eventually settle down to a legit family life, if they can just earn enough from the next big score. Of the two, Jason is definitely the duller partner. An ex-military meathead with a ripped body and a dull, affect-free vocal delivery, a decent chunk of Jason’s lines essentially boil down to “Yeah, sure, that’s fine.” While the game struggles to expose a bit of a tender and thoughtful side hiding underneath Jason’s cool demeanor, the writing can’t quite break through the emotionless masculine facade that Jason wears as a semi-permanent mask. Lucia is much more interesting as a vivacious and amiable Latina eager to grab any opportunity presented to her. The game takes some time to dig into the difficulties of Lucia’s underprivileged youth and highlight her strained relationship with an unreliable mother, helping to add some important depth to her chip-on-her-shoulder journey of self-improvement. And even the boring Jason seems that much more appealing seen through the lens of Lucia’s good-natured teasing and genuine affection. While Jason and Lucia can and do operate independently—and the game lets you change between them frequently—it’s their moments of togetherness that really stand out. There’s an easy, rom-com comfort to their time together, whether they’re discussing their future on the couch (“I feel like I haven’t done anything normal in a minute”), taking some time for quick romance (the game cuts away before things get too hot and heavy), or laying down covering fire for each other during a firefight (the lack of a co-op mode for these missions feels truly baffling). There’s a minor relationship simulation component to the game, with a simple “heart level” that can rise or fall based on some basic decisions. Don’t expect a lot of dating-sim style drama, though; as long as you make the completely obvious choices when they’re presented, it’s hard to let the relationship fall apart. That’s a good thing, too, because this is a relationship that’s easy to root for, even when the participants are literally getting away with murder. In true Grand Theft Auto fashion, Jason and Lucia’s particular way of chasing The American Dream is through a life of crime. Their travels through the criminal underworld start off kind of slow, as Lucia’s begging gradually compels Jason to reluctantly introduce her to the two-bit operators with which he’s found himself involved. For the first half of the game, the pair are constantly interacting with a rogues’ gallery of new criminal acquaintances, each more over-the-top than the last, and all of them having specific needs that somehow only Jason and Lucia can fulfill. Many of the missions these small-time crooks have on offer end up feeling like the criminal equivalent of errands—drive here, take that, lose the cops, repeat. It isn’t until the back half of the game that the main storyline really starts to focus on what it does best: integrating Jason and Lucia into a persistent ring of professional criminals working toward bigger and bigger scores. Here, the missions build on each other, with characters going undercover, casing targets, and learning new skills that eventually come together in some truly tense and bombastic heists. These missions also do the best job of showing off the dual protagonist system, frequently shifting the perspective between Jason and Lucia to highlight their different skills and views on how things are going down. Outside of this core plot, though, many of the missions and side stories in GTA VI make Jason and Lucia feel like side characters in their own story. I found myself beginning to tune out during some of the many missions in which one or both protagonists serve as glorified security props or overpaid getaway drivers amid other characters’ contrived turf wars. And even dozens of hours into the game, there were still missions that felt like tutorials, seemingly built around the opportunity to introduce some new simulation system or control scheme. Through it all, the game can’t seem to totally shake the style of sophomoric humor that feels a lot less “edgy” today than it did when Grand Theft Auto III hit back in 2001 (for players who are old enough to remember that release , at least). There are countless extended bits where the entire joke seems to boil down to “Man, kinky sex is weird, isn’t it?” or “Hey look, it’s a male penis (or something that looks similar to one).” And the game seems to take particular pleasure in forcing Jason into uncomfortable situations with plenty of T&A, much to Lucia’s good-natured bemusement. A word of warning for parents: This is a game that definitely earns a hard “M for Mature” rating and shows how standards for that rating have shifted since GTA: San Andreas earned an AO re-rating for hiding a single sex scene amid its legacy code. There are moments where GTA VI ’s satire cuts a bit deeper. I especially liked a couple of side stories that skewered buzzword-spewing crypto bros and multi-level marketing schemes with some welcome over-the-top excess. Overall, though, the game’s warmed-over one-liner takes on “wokeness” felt about as fresh as jokes about mothers-in-law and TV dinners, without much in the way of thought-provoking statements on society as a whole in 2026. Grand Theft Auto VI has a gift for finding excuses to lure you into an expertly designed space and then throwing together a reason for why you have to shoot/punch your way out. That might sound snarky, but I actually mean it more or less sincerely; I was frequently surprised by the scenarios the writers dreamed up to turn what seemed like a routine trip to some beautiful locale into a firefight with way more armed goons than seems strictly necessary. The moment-to-moment shooting will feel very familiar to Grand Theft Auto fans, by which I mean it’s dead simple to hide behind convenient cover and pop up to pick off relatively stupid enemies one by one with a dizzying array of available weaponry. The rare enemies that do manage to flank you seem to have incredibly bad aim, even at close range, and both Jason and Lucia can take a whole lot more punishment than the average quick-to-crumble grunt. Driving around town is significantly more exciting—you’ll be darting between cars in heavy traffic to chase down antagonists, avoid the police, or simply get where you’re going faster. It’s still a blast to sample as many vehicles as you can, from zippy but easy-to-wreck sports cars to tank-like trucks that can plow through traffic, tiny motorbikes that can squeeze through tight spaces, and off-road vehicles that can explore off the beaten path. Driving through the city also offers ample opportunities to get distracted from your main goals by dozens of side activities that dot the map. Even as I struggled to work through the story on deadline, I found myself getting sucked in for hours trying to master drone racing, chasing gold medals in countless mud-splattered rally races, or hunting for one of the many meditation spots hidden in out-of-the-way corners. While most of these side activities offer money or improve character stats, some are simply there to be experienced. Completionists will have a bear of a time tracking down every single hidden collectible, rare car, robbable location, and beautiful landmark the developers have placed throughout the city. Grand Theft Auto VI seems set to be one of those games you can just load up to hang out in long after the main story missions are done. Even with a fast vehicle, much of that “hang out” time can be spent simply crossing the game’s massive map. Getting from the depths of the wilderness in the north to the tip of the keys in the south is a six-plus-mile trip (measured at an apparently real-world-accurate scale) that can take 10 minutes to weave your way across on a good traffic day. During these cross-city treks, the tenor of the city’s architecture morphs noticeably as you pass from rich gated communities through the glitzy skyscraper-laden downtown and on to downtrodden neighborhoods, backwoods swamps, and laid-back island beach communities. As nice as Vice City’s outdoor architecture is, GTA VI’ s interiors are where the game’s developers really show off. Practically every story mission seems to introduce a new cavernous indoor space that’s fully furnished and lovingly crafted to look naturally lived-in and also utterly unlike anything you’ve seen before. And while you can’t go into every one of the thousands of buildings you pass on the streets of Vice City, you can enter a surprisingly large number, each with its own distinct layout and decorations. Another element that makes all these spaces feel lived-in is the game’s surprisingly detailed crowd system. Grand Theft Auto VI sometimes packs over a hundred non-player characters into a single space, with no two characters looking or acting alike in size, shape, dress, or animation. Working your way through these crowds can be integral to some of the game’s missions, but even when you’re just casually exploring, it’s fun to take advantage of eavesdropping opportunities, listening in on individual conversations that build into overlapping chatter (realistically muffled through walls and over distance). Grand Theft Auto VI ’s spaces also seem specifically designed to show off the game’s incredible lighting system, which really shines on a PS5 Pro. The effect is most apparent at night, when car headlights streaming through a window or the rotating blue-and-red of a cop car can cast the entire world in an otherworldly glow. But even in “normal” lighting conditions, I’d occasionally find myself slack-jawed at the details: a laptop screen partially reflected in a character’s glasses, the way rotating pyrotechnic laser effects played across dancers in a crowded club, the fluttering shadows cast by a leafy tree near sunset, or the finger smudges visible on your cell phone in bright sunshine. I could go on and on about the little “attention to detail” touches that add up to a more engaging world simulation. Characters who fall in the dirt get dust on only the specific parts of their clothes that hit the ground. Older characters look distinctly wrinkly, with veins that show through their thinning skin. Fabric and hair flow naturally in the wind and as characters move. Rain beads on car roofs and drips off overhangs during a storm. Through it all, one moment really stood out to me. As I prepared for an upcoming firefight, I had Lucia start eating some chips to buff her health. Halfway through the bag, I had her pick up a nearby soda, too. At first, Lucia held the chip bag in one hand and used the other to pick out individual chips. But once that other hand was occupied with a soda, she started shaking the bag above her head to pour the chips directly into her mouth. When I thought about the effort that went into coding and recording that specific animation for such a highly specific edge case, I thought about the millions of man-hours that went into making Grand Theft Auto VI the ultimate expression of this kind of urban crime/life sim. It might be a long time before we see this level of focused effort on a singular interactive vision again. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.
