extraction.body: As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments. The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital. Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks , but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups including Mecka AI , XDOF , and MicroAGI are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them. Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) said in an interview. Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN . KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch. Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from. “Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal said. Humyn Labs says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers. The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized. That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said. Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups including Human Archive and BuildAI tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes. Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated. Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said. Humyn Labs raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies train models that operate in physical environments. The Bengaluru startup collects and processes footage of people performing everyday tasks, then sells that data to customers building robots.

The financing includes $26 million in equity and $21 million in venture debt. Accel led the equity round. Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance's Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading joined. Lighthouse Canton Growth Debt Fund II led the debt, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

Companies worldwide build robots for everyday human tasks, but they struggle to obtain enough quality training data. Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI already collect real-world robotics data. Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.

Humyn Labs built its own two-camera hardware to record people at work and at home. The company's software processes and labels the footage, tagging events in each clip so AI systems can learn from them. The startup collects data in more than 20 countries across Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal said.

Agarwal, the former CEO of Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta, a former executive at AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN's contributor network across emerging markets helps Humyn Labs collect data inside homes.

Recording footage covers part of the job, Agarwal said. Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, object interactions, and other details, converting raw video into structured data for AI models. "Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem," Agarwal said.

Twelve paying customers buy from Humyn Labs. They include frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. U.S. customers generate about 90% of revenue, Gupta said, though he declined to name customers. The startup generated $10 million in revenue from April through October and holds $20 million in signed contracts. Agarwal said another $20 million in deals has not reached final terms.

The new contracts increased working-capital needs, Agarwal said. Humyn Labs pays workers and collection partners daily or weekly, but customers often pay 30 to 60 days later. The $21 million debt bridges that gap and dilutes ownership less than selling more equity.

India now serves as a hub for collecting training data for physical AI. Startups such as Human Archive and BuildAI recruit workers to record everyday tasks. The practice raises privacy and consent questions, especially when companies record people inside homes.

Agarwal said Humyn Labs records people doing their usual work or household chores rather than staged activities. Local partners identify collection sites and supervise the process. "The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input," he said.
Humyn Labs employs 51 full-time staff, most in Bengaluru, plus local partners in collection countries.

The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital. Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers. That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said. Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups including Human Archive and BuildAI tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. LAS VEGAS — The HHS Office for Civil Rights finalized modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule on Monday, aimed at increasing patients’ access to their own medical records. The rule, initially proposed in 2020, contains a slew of substantive updates to the foundational health data privacy rule that seek to reduce administrative friction and encourage health data sharing. The final rule slashes the timeframe for providers to respond to patient record requests in half, from 30 calendar days to 15. It also enables providers to share more health information with certain third parties, like social workers, in a play to enhance care coordination. And in line with the Trump administration’s enthusiasm for patient access to digital health tools , patients will also be able to obtain copies of their records via health apps. “I know that lots of people have been looking forward to this rule. Some believe that it should have been done much earlier,” OCR Director Paula Stannard said during a session at the HLTH 2026 conference. “But we are convinced that this will provide individuals with faster access to health information while at the same time facilitating health information interoperability, enhancing care coordination, reducing regulatory burden and protecting the privacy of individual health information as we seek to improve the healthcare system by making information more interoperable.” The rule will go into effect 60 days after it’s published on the federal register, which is set to happen on Thursday. Healthcare providers, payers and their business associates will be expected to comply around July 10, or roughly six months after the effective date. The HHS estimates that the rule will result in $784 million in new costs within a year of implementation, but that those upfront costs will be offset by net cost savings of $703 million annually in years two through five. The department says the majority of the savings will come from eliminating the requirement that healthcare providers obtain a signed acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of privacy practices, which the HHS says currently costs providers significant time and money. When HIPAA was enacted in 1996, the commercial internet was in its infancy and electronic health records were not yet widely adopted. The regulation initially set out to help people transfer health insurance when they switched jobs and to standardize health information, but it later evolved to set standards for privacy and security in the sector. Since the HIPAA Privacy Rule was tacked onto the law in 2003, it has served as the preeminent federal regulation for safeguarding the privacy and confidentiality of protected health information transmitted by providers, payers and their business associates. It sets strict parameters for how and when healthcare organizations can use or disclose PHI and gives patients the right to request access to their records, mandating that they receive them in a timely manner. Giving patients access to their medical records has been a priority under President Donald Trump’s OCR, and remains one of the top complaints the agency receives . During his first administration, the OCR launched an enforcement initiative to discipline providers that fail to provide patients timely access to their records, and the agency has cracked down on 55 organizations over the last seven years. The new rule smooths the road for providers to share health records with patients by adding definitions for “personal health application” and “electronic health record,” two terms that HIPAA had never explicitly defined before. Before, providers faced significant uncertainty about permitting health apps to access patient records because it was unclear whether patient data would be at risk once records were sent to an app that isn’t covered by HIPAA. Now, the rule’s tightened language gives providers a clearer path to send health data to apps. It plainly states that if a patient asks for their records to be sent to a health app that meets the agency’s definitions, they must do so. A personal health application, according to the final rule, is an app used by an individual to access their own health information, even if that information is drawn from multiple sources. The app must be controlled by that individual, rather than an organization or another person. Commenters on the proposed rule were divided on whether the personal health app definition should be broader, covering more platforms and use cases, or narrower, to only include apps that met strict security and privacy standards. The HHS largely finalized the provision as proposed, without adding additional security limits, taking a broader approach. An electronic health record, in the eyes of HIPAA, is now formally defined as an electronic record of “health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff,” the rule states. Among the rule’s many other elements is a provision that prohibits entities from imposing “unreasonable” identity verification requirements on an individual wanting to access their health records, such as requiring a patient to appear in person when there’s a method for remote verification available. Organizations must also start posting the cost of obtaining medical records on their websites. Days before the rule was finalized, a coalition of healthcare executives wrote a letter to HHS asking it not to finalize the rule on the grounds that certain provisions would make it difficult for providers to confirm whether a third-party application has been authorized by a patient to receive their PHI. They also raised concerns about the move to loosen the verification requirements. Despite the security concerns, the rule was finalized largely as proposed. The HIPAA Security Rule, the privacy rule’s sister regulation that sets standards for the protection of electronic health information, is also due for a long-anticipated update next summer . passages: CHICAGO — A new examination of patient perspectives on data privacy illustrates unresolved tension over the eroding security and confidentiality of personal health information in a wired society and economy.
More than 92% of patients believe privacy is a right and their health data should not be available for purchase, according to a survey (PDF) released today by the American Medical Association (AMA).

As the only medical association that convenes 190+ state and specialty medical societies and other critical stakeholders, the AMA represents physicians with a unified voice to all key players in health care.
Jackson Women’s Health Organization as the lack of data privacy could place patients and physicians in legal peril in states that restrict reproductive health services.
“Patients trust that physicians are committed to protecting patient privacy—a crucial element for honest health discussions,” said AMA President Jack Resneck Jr., M.D.
“Many digital health technologies, however, lack even basic privacy safeguards.
More must be done by policymakers and developers to protect patients’ health information.
Most health apps are either unregulated or underregulated, requiring near and long-term policy initiatives and robust enforcement by federal and state regulators.
About three out of five patients (59%) expressed concern with personal health data being used against them or their loved ones.
Patients also want physicians and their hospitals to have the technology and capability to review apps for privacy and security protections.
Strong regulations are needed to support patients’ right to data privacy and restore trust in data exchange that facilitates accessible, equitable, and personalized care.
Patients must have meaningful control and a clear understanding of how their data is being used and with whom it is being shared.
The AMA’s Privacy Principles (PDF) outline five key aspects of a national privacy framework—individual rights, equity, entity responsibility, applicability, and enforcement.
The AMA has also developed a guide (PDF) to help app developers build privacy-forward technologies.

The AMA continues to advocate for near-term app transparency requirements, including app privacy attestations collected by EHRs , that will increase transparency and bolster individuals’ choice in which apps to use.
As Congress continues discussions around federal privacy legislation, the AMA seeks to ensure that resulting privacy law protects the sacred trust at the heart of the physician-patient relationship.
A federal process to gain feedback on proposed regulations offers medical students a voice in health policy.
Details provided on the application process and deadlines for physicians, residents and medical students interested in joining AMA council and committees.

coreStoryFacts.text: LAS VEGAS — The HHS Office for Civil Rights finalized modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule on Monday, aimed at increasing patients’ access to their own medical records.
When HIPAA was enacted in 1996, the commercial internet was in its infancy and electronic health records were not yet widely adopted.

The regulation initially set out to help people transfer health insurance when they switched jobs and to standardize health information, but it later evolved to set standards for privacy and security in the sector.

“But we are convinced that this will provide individuals with faster access to health information while at the same time facilitating health information interoperability, enhancing care coordination, reducing regulatory burden and protecting the privacy of individual health information as we seek to improve the healthcare system by making information more interoperable.”

Commenters on the proposed rule were divided on whether the personal health app definition should be broader, covering more platforms and use cases, or narrower, to only include apps that met strict security and privacy standards.
Let Healthcare Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.
The final rule slashes the timeframe for providers to respond to patient record requests in half, from 30 calendar days to 15.
And in line with the Trump administration’s enthusiasm for patient access to digital health tools , patients will also be able to obtain copies of their records via health apps.

Before, providers faced significant uncertainty about permitting health apps to access patient records because it was unclear whether patient data would be at risk once records were sent to an app that isn’t covered by HIPAA.
Now, the rule’s tightened language gives providers a clearer path to send health data to apps.

An electronic health record, in the eyes of HIPAA, is now formally defined as an electronic record of “health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff,” the rule states.

The department says the majority of the savings will come from eliminating the requirement that healthcare providers obtain a signed acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of privacy practices, which the HHS says currently costs providers significant time and money.

LAS VEGAS — The HHS Office for Civil Rights finalized modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule on Monday, aimed at increasing patients’ access to their own medical records. The rule, initially proposed in 2020, contains a slew of substantive updates to the foundational health data privacy rule that seek to reduce administrative friction and encourage health data sharing. The final rule slashes the timeframe for providers to respond to patient record requests in half, from 30 calendar days to 15. It also enables providers to share more health information with certain third parties, like social workers, in a play to enhance care coordination. And in line with the Trump administration’s enthusiasm for patient access to digital health tools , patients will also be able to obtain copies of their records via health apps. “I know that lots of people have been looking forward to this rule. Some believe that it should have been done much earlier,” OCR Director Paula Stannard said during a session at the HLTH 2026 conference. “But we are convinced that this will provide individuals with faster access to health information while at the same time facilitating health information interoperability, enhancing care coordination, reducing regulatory burden and protecting the privacy of individual health information as we seek to improve the healthcare system by making information more interoperable.” The rule will go into effect 60 days after it’s published on the federal register, which is set to happen on Thursday. Healthcare providers, payers and their business associates will be expected to comply around July 10, or roughly six months after the effective date. The HHS estimates that the rule will result in $784 million in new costs within a year of implementation, but that those upfront costs will be offset by net cost savings of $703 million annually in years two through five. The department says the majority of the savings will come from eliminating the requirement that healthcare providers obtain a signed acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of privacy practices, which the HHS says currently costs providers significant time and money. When HIPAA was enacted in 1996, the commercial internet was in its infancy and electronic health records were not yet widely adopted. The regulation initially set out to help people transfer health insurance when they switched jobs and to standardize health information, but it later evolved to set standards for privacy and security in the sector. Since the HIPAA Privacy Rule was tacked onto the law in 2003, it has served as the preeminent federal regulation for safeguarding the privacy and confidentiality of protected health information transmitted by providers, payers and their business associates. It sets strict parameters for how and when healthcare organizations can use or disclose PHI and gives patients the right to request access to their records, mandating that they receive them in a timely manner. Giving patients access to their medical records has been a priority under President Donald Trump’s OCR, and remains one of the top complaints the agency receives . During his first administration, the OCR launched an enforcement initiative to discipline providers that fail to provide patients timely access to their records, and the agency has cracked down on 55 organizations over the last seven years. The new rule smooths the road for providers to share health records with patients by adding definitions for “personal health application” and “electronic health record,” two terms that HIPAA had never explicitly defined before. Before, providers faced significant uncertainty about permitting health apps to access patient records because it was unclear whether patient data would be at risk once records were sent to an app that isn’t covered by HIPAA. Now, the rule’s tightened language gives providers a clearer path to send health data to apps. It plainly states that if a patient asks for their records to be sent to a health app that meets the agency’s definitions, they must do so. A personal health application, according to the final rule, is an app used by an individual to access their own health information, even if that information is drawn from multiple sources. The app must be controlled by that individual, rather than an organization or another person. Commenters on the proposed rule were divided on whether the personal health app definition should be broader, covering more platforms and use cases, or narrower, to only include apps that met strict security and privacy standards. The HHS largely finalized the provision as proposed, without adding additional security limits, taking a broader approach. An electronic health record, in the eyes of HIPAA, is now formally defined as an electronic record of “health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff,” the rule states. Among the rule’s many other elements is a provision that prohibits entities from imposing “unreasonable” identity verification requirements on an individual wanting to access their health records, such as requiring a patient to appear in person when there’s a method for remote verification available. Organizations must also start posting the cost of obtaining medical records on their websites. Days before the rule was finalized, a coalition of healthcare executives wrote a letter to HHS asking it not to finalize the rule on the grounds that certain provisions would make it difficult for providers to confirm whether a third-party application has been authorized by a patient to receive their PHI. They also raised concerns about the move to loosen the verification requirements. Despite the security concerns, the rule was finalized largely as proposed. The HIPAA Security Rule, the privacy rule’s sister regulation that sets standards for the protection of electronic health information, is also due for a long-anticipated update next summer . CHICAGO — A new examination of patient perspectives on data privacy illustrates unresolved tension over the eroding security and confidentiality of personal health information in a wired society and economy. More than 92% of patients believe privacy is a right and their health data should not be available for purchase, according to a survey (PDF) released today by the American Medical Association (AMA).

The survey of 1,000 patients was conducted by Savvy Cooperative, a patient-owned source of health care insights, at the beginning of 2022 and found concern over data privacy protections and confusion regarding who can access personal health information. Nearly 75% of patients expressed concern about protecting the privacy of personal health data, and only 20% of patients indicated they knew the scope of companies and individuals with access to their data. This concern is magnified with the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization as the lack of data privacy could place patients and physicians in legal peril in states that restrict reproductive health services.

The survey indicated patients are most comfortable with physicians and hospitals having access to personal health data, and least comfortable with social media sites, employers and technology companies having access to the same data.

“Patients trust that physicians are committed to protecting patient privacy—a crucial element for honest health discussions,” said AMA President Jack Resneck Jr., M.D. “Many digital health technologies, however, lack even basic privacy safeguards. More must be done by policymakers and developers to protect patients’ health information. Most health apps are either unregulated or underregulated, requiring near and long-term policy initiatives and robust enforcement by federal and state regulators. Patient confidence in data privacy is undermined as technology companies and data brokers gain access to indelible health data without patient knowledge or consent and share this information with third parties, including law enforcement.”

The survey found an overwhelming percentage of patients demand accountability, transparency, and control as it relates to health data privacy. More than nine out of ten (94%) patients want companies to be held legally accountable for uses of their health data. A similar majority of patients (93%) want health application (app) developers to be transparent about how their products use and share personal health data. To prevent unwanted access and use of personal health data, patients want control over what companies collected about them and how it is used:

Patients worry about the repercussions of little or no control over the use and sharing of personal health data that companies have collected. About three out of five patients (59%) expressed concern with personal health data being used against them or their loved ones. Most patients stated they are “very” or “extremely” concerned about discriminatory uses of personal health data to exclude them from insurance coverage (64%), employment (56%), or opportunities for health care (59%). More than half of Hispanic/Latinx and American Indian or Alaskan Natives stated they are “highly” concerned about discriminatory uses of personal health data and two-thirds (66%) of transgender individuals stated they are “extremely” concerned.

Patients also want physicians and their hospitals to have the technology and capability to review apps for privacy and security protections. Nearly nine out of ten (88%) patients believe that their doctor or hospital should have the ability to review and verify the security of health apps before those apps gain access to their health data. Unfortunately, federal regulations prevent providers and even electronic health record (EHR) systems from conducting necessary privacy and security reviews of apps.

Strong regulations are needed to support patients’ right to data privacy and restore trust in data exchange that facilitates accessible, equitable, and personalized care. Patients must have meaningful control and a clear understanding of how their data is being used and with whom it is being shared. The AMA’s Privacy Principles (PDF) outline five key aspects of a national privacy framework—individual rights, equity, entity responsibility, applicability, and enforcement. The AMA has also developed a guide (PDF) to help app developers build privacy-forward technologies. The AMA continues to advocate for near-term app transparency requirements, including app privacy attestations collected by EHRs , that will increase transparency and bolster individuals’ choice in which apps to use. As Congress continues discussions around federal privacy legislation, the AMA seeks to ensure that resulting privacy law protects the sacred trust at the heart of the physician-patient relationship.

As the only medical association that convenes 190+ state and specialty medical societies and other critical stakeholders, the AMA represents physicians with a unified voice to all key players in health care.
